#6424. A natural varnish was discovered on 37,000-year-old horse paintings in Chauvet Cave using ultraviolet light

A UV probe used from up to 8 feet (2.5 meters) away found a translucent calcite layer over the 37,000-year-old charcoal horses of Chauvet Cave.

In Chauvet Cave, in the Ardèche gorge of southern France, researchers set up a tripod on the steel walkway in the Hillaire Chamber and ran a carbon fiber pole out toward the Horses Panel.

Artists drew those horses in charcoal about 37,000 years ago. A lens at the pole’s tip sat 2 inches (5 centimeters) off the rock and lit it with ultraviolet light. The operator, meanwhile, stayed up to 8 feet (2.5 meters) back on the walkway.

What came back showed a translucent skin of calcite over parts of the black lines. The team called it a natural varnish and plotted the spots where it shows on the panel. Still, the survey cannot say how thick it is.

Jean-Marie Chauvet, Éliette Brunel and Christian Hillaire got into the cave on Sunday, December 18, 1994, according to the French Ministry of Culture, and on Christmas Eve they went back and put a plastic strip down over the path they had used.

The steel walkways follow that strip today. Per the ministry’s page on the cave layout, they are 2 feet (60 centimeters) wide. In the main chambers, they run for 1,214 feet (370 meters). Crews also widened the old entrance and fitted it with a heavy reinforced door.

There are animal tracks and human footprints on the floor, so everyone works from the walkways only. The paper puts the walls 3 to 20 feet (1 to 6 meters) away from them. At the panels in this study, the gap is 5 to 10 feet (1.5 to 3 meters).

At that range the team ruled out X-ray fluorescence and Raman spectroscopy, the standard pigment tools. Neither can tell bedrock limestone from calcite left later by dripping water anyway, as both are calcite.

First author Yohan Boulard works at LAMS, the Laboratory of Molecular and Structural Archaeology of Sorbonne University and the CNRS in Paris. He designed the instrument with Thiéry Guillou and Philippe Walter, the corresponding author.

Light came from a 1.3-watt OSRAM LED at 365 nanometers. It went up the pole through one of seven fibers in a 10-foot (3-meter) bundle, and the other six carried the glow back to an Ocean Optics USB4000 spectrometer, with a 24-volt battery for power and a Python program on a laptop to log each reading.

Dyed papers left under the beam did not fade. So the team took the light as safe for the walls. Humidity in the chamber ran at about 100 percent, at 55 degrees Fahrenheit (13 degrees Celsius).

In the lab, calcite sampled from Chauvet for earlier work glowed with one blue peak, near 450 nanometers. However, limestone from near the site showed that peak and another near 580.

When the team dissolved the calcite in hydrochloric acid, the blue stayed in the liquid. That tied it to organic matter from the surface ecosystem.

Carole Fritz, of LAMS and the CREAP center in Toulouse, led the cave’s scientific team. She also supervised the study with Walter and Maguy Jaber. The group took 60 spectra in all, 47 of them on the Horses Panel.

Over the black lines the signal dropped to as little as one-twentieth of what bare rock gave. Charcoal soaks up ultraviolet light without glowing, so any light at all off a line meant something was lying over it.

The lip of the central horse gave almost only the blue calcite peak. Bare limestone beside it gave both peaks, and the jaw, where the charcoal covers the rock only in part, fell in between.

The authors pointed out that thick crusts can hide paintings but a clear one can “behave like a natural varnish.” For example, at Arcy-sur-Cure’s Grande Grotte in the Yonne department, an opaque calcite crust hid the Paleolithic paintings. They stayed hidden until restorers rubbed it off.

Uranium-thorium dates on such crusts were used to claim that Neanderthals made cave art in Spain more than 64,000 years ago, and a long list of rock art specialists rejected that reading in a 2020 paper in the Journal of Human Evolution.

The Alcove of the Lions, in the same sector as the Horses Panel, gave a different picture. Water got in there after people left the cave, and it left flowstone, calcite laid down in sheets where water runs over rock.

The team recorded eleven spectra in the alcove. On the left, flowstone pours out of a horizontal crack that crosses a horse’s head. Over that head, the blue glow was bright enough to show in the photographs.

Farther down, on a horse’s breast, the calcite grew on bare rock and stopped at the charcoal lines. Those lines gave no calcite signal at all.

The team took this as a sign that the charcoal affected how the crystals formed. Earlier work on iron and manganese oxide pigments, by contrast, found no such link.

Seeping water also coated the Signs Panel in Chauvet’s Red Panel Chamber, according to the ministry, and the same mineral builds the stalagmites that rise from cave floors.

Some charcoal marks had orange patches just under them in the ultraviolet photographs, and the spectra from those spots peaked near 580 nanometers.

The team burned Scots pine at 752, 932 and 1,292 degrees Fahrenheit (400, 500 and 700 degrees Celsius) to make test charcoal, because the cave’s own charcoal came from that tree, as an earlier study in Antiquity found. Its tar glowed blue.

The team also heated limestone and calcite samples to 932 degrees Fahrenheit (500 degrees Celsius) for one hour or 24 hours. Afterward, they glowed orange. The same orange showed up near torch smears, the marks people left on the wall when they revived a torch.

The authors suggested that some lines were drawn with charcoal that had “hot, possibly burning tips,” and they wrote that this is not direct proof.

At Font-de-Gaume, another French cave, charcoal from black drawings has been used for dating, to between 13,000 and 16,000 years ago.

There is no thickness for the varnish in the paper, in millimeters or anything else. Nobody made calcite layers of known thickness to calibrate against. The authors also wrote that grown layers like the cave’s would be very hard to copy.

The blue signal depends on both the thickness of the calcite and how much organic matter it holds. In the Alcove of the Lions, flowstone and thin veils formed in different ways. So nobody can compare the numbers there one to one.

The burning-charcoal idea still needs testing. For example, studies could look at how far the charcoal burned. They could also test how heat changes clays with more or less iron oxide. Also, the survey covered only one sector of the cave, the Horses Sector.

The authors called the method “a promising tool” for deciding how decorated caves are protected and who gets in. For now, the readings taken from the Hillaire Chamber walkway show a translucent calcite layer over the horses.

The full study was published in the journal ACS Omega.

A stunning fossil owl from Germany that has its last meal preserved in its stomach helped researchers to narrow down the time when these birds mostly became active at night.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A fledgling owl that lived 47 million years ago in what is now Germany offers tantalizing new clues about when most of these birds became nocturnal, a new study shows. The discovery brings researchers one step closer to finally solving the biggest mystery about these birds.

The young owl is a newly described species named Masillastrix blattophaga. Researchers unearthed the almost perfectly preserved bird in 2025 in the Messel Pit, an ancient lake surrounded by a forest that is now the richest fossil site in the world for understanding life in the Eocene epoch (56 million to 34 million years ago). The skull is missing, but the rest of the fossil was so well preserved that researchers found the owl's last meal in its stomach: a greenish-blue, iridescent cockroach.

The cockroach is one of several pieces of evidence suggesting that this tiny owl was diurnal, or active primarily during the day. Iridescence is associated with a diurnal lifestyle, so it appears that the owl, which measured less than 5 inches (12 centimeters) long, was hunting in the daytime, researchers said in the new study.

This indicates that owls were not nocturnal 47 million years ago and so must have switched to the night-owl lifestyle more recently, said study first author Gerald Mayr, a paleontologist and head of ornithology at the Senckenberg Research Institute and the Natural History Museum Frankfurt in Germany.

"There exists a consensus that owls must have evolved from a diurnal ancestor," Mayr told Live Science in an email. That's because some early owl fossils have head-rotation structures similar to those of diurnal raptors and bony ridges above the eye sockets that could have shaded the owls' eyes from the sun.

Therefore, it is plausible that the Messel owl was fully diurnal, rather than active during the daytime and nighttime as some owls are today, because that would imply that some of its ancestors had already evolved nocturnal traits, Mayr said.

Researchers also found a cockroach identical to the one in the Messel owl's stomach in sediments just a few feet away from the new fossil. This well-preserved cockroach helped the team to identify the insect inside the owl, the researchers wrote in the study, which was published Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It's possible that the owl ate the cockroach at dawn or at dusk, which might cast doubt on whether the bird was diurnal. But there are other clues hinting that the owl was diurnal, including the appearance of some of the owl's feathers and the stoutness of its upper wing bones.

Mayr said he and his colleagues believe the shape of the upper wing bones, or humeri, is an indicator of when owls are active. The Messel owl's stocky humeri hint that the species flew during the day, when silent movement doesn't confer a significant advantage because there is enough light to see predators. Conversely, modern nocturnal owls have slim humeri and fly almost soundlessly, he said.

The fossil was so well preserved that researchers identified a cockroach in the stomach that was likely the owl's last meal.

Assuming this hypothesis is correct, the earliest known nocturnal owl species are from about 35 million years ago, in the Late Eocene, Mayr said. Owl fossils from this period and more recently look a lot like modern owls and have elongated humeri, he noted. The oldest known owl in the fossil record, Ogygoptynx wetmorei, dates to around 60 million years ago.

This means that owls likely became nocturnal between 47 million and 35 million years ago. This is the best current estimate, because the owl fossil record is very sparse and species are often described from only a few isolated bones, according to the study.

"We still know so little about the early evolution of modern birds," Mayr said, adding that every fossil discovery has the power to change even well-established ideas in the field.

The big question that remains is why owls became nocturnal. Previous theories suggested that owls evolved this behavior to avoid competition with diurnal birds of prey or to benefit from a proliferation of nocturnal mammals. But studies show that both of these groups exploded much later than 35 million years ago — around 20 million to 25 million years ago — suggesting there wasn't a clear advantage driving owls to switch to nocturnal lifestyles at that time.

The new results have deepened the uncertainty of why owls turned nocturnal. But "by narrowing down the time frame when owls became nocturnal, our study may eventually contribute to solving this mystery," Mayr said.

Mayr, G., Šmídová, L., Richter, A., & Wedmann, S. (2026). Evidence for diurnal habits in an exceptionally preserved Eocene owl. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.09.079

Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Southampton in England and a master’s degree in science communication from Imperial College London. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.

#6421. Tracking water in real time could help scientists catch harmful algal blooms before they spread

DNA read from Florida lagoon water turned up 11 kinds of harmful algae, most at trace levels and often several at one site.

A red tide looks like something that arrives. One week the water is clear, and the next it’s stained and fish are washing up dead. In a lagoon on Florida’s east coast, the algae behind it were there the whole time.

Researchers who read the DNA in the lagoon’s water found 11 kinds of harmful algae, each a species known to cause blooms. Most were at levels so low that a microscope would likely have missed them, and they tended to turn up in the same places.

Finding them together is the surprise. Several harmful species sharing one stretch of water suggests they answer to the same triggers or help each other grow.

Justin Gibbons, a computational biologist at the USF College of Public Health, led the work with Rays H.Y. Jiang, an associate professor of genomics there.

Research colleagues came from Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.

The water was collected in 2018 and 2019, and the method has not yet been tested as a way to warn of a bloom ahead of time.

The Indian River Lagoon runs 156 miles (251 kilometers) along the coast, from a temperate climate in the north to a subtropical one in the south. The team sampled 20 sites along it in the wet season of 2018 and again in the dry season of 2019.

At each site, three 17-ounce (500 milliliter) bottles were filled below the surface and chilled. The water was filtered within six hours, and the team pulled DNA off the filters. The river DNA test lists every species that shed cells upstream.

The sequencer was a MinION, a palm-sized, portable device that reads long stretches of DNA. Microbial monitoring often reads a bacterial gene called 16S.

Algae aren’t bacteria, so the team read a gene called 18S, which cells with a nucleus carry, and they read it nearly end to end.

In an interview with Earth.com, Jiang said that choice covers a blind spot in bloom monitoring. “Full-length 18S helps reveal the culprits.”

Across four sequencing runs, the team identified more than 200 named species. Between a third and 45 percent of the reads matched nothing in the reference library, so the true count may be higher.

Each species was then checked against the harmful algae list kept by UNESCO’s oceanographic commission. Eleven matched, counting the brown tide species that the team added to the list, and two stood out.

Brown tide alga Aureoumbra lagunensis appeared in 13 of the 40 samples. In the northern lagoon and the Banana River, it reached more than half of all the DNA reads at some sites, with its highest levels in the dry season.

Biologists counting cells in the Banana River had recorded an unusually long brown tide there across 2018 and 2019.

Northern stretches are where the lagoon’s trouble has concentrated. They take nitrogen from household septic tanks and hold their water longer than the south does, and they suffered a large-scale seagrass die-off in the 2010s.

Of every stretch sampled, the Banana River had the lowest diversity and the highest share of harmful algae species.

Pyrodinium bahamense, which makes the nerve poison saxitoxin, showed up at four northern sites in the wet season and at none in the dry season. It reached at most 4 percent of the reads.

Toxin sampling from the same places and months had found saxitoxin too.

Nine other harmful species each stayed below 1 percent. One of them, Gonyaulax bohaiensis, had not been recorded in North America before, and it turned up at seven sites.

“The result that stood out to me the most was the frequent co-occurrence of the harmful algal bloom species,” Gibbons said.

“This suggests that there’s either shared ecological drivers for them or that they somehow interact and promote the growth of each other.”

Most stretches of the lagoon held more than one harmful species. Asked what surprised her about species showing up together, Jiang told Earth.com that she kept her answer to the forecasting problem.

“A bloom is a community response, not just one species,” she said. “Forecasting needs to capture that complexity.”

In the same interview, Greg O’Corry-Crowe, a research professor at Harbor Branch, said the physical and chemical triggers have had most of the attention so far.

“A major challenge is understanding what the triggers are that lead to periodic explosive growth, where the benign becomes the harmful,” he said.

A read count is a share, not a cell count. The MinION misreads more letters than the standard lab sequencers do, so the team wrote that the rarest detections should be treated with caution.

The primers that copy the gene may also favor some species over others.

Two samples came from water so cloudy with a Pyrodinium bloom that less of it could be filtered, and the rarest species there may have been missed.

One toxic diatom group that is common in the lagoon, Pseudo-nitzschia, appeared only when the team searched at the genus level.

The samples are also seven to eight years old. Whether a reading taken at the water’s edge can flag a bloom before anyone sees one is the claim the study sets up and does not test.

Monitoring programs already count cells under a microscope and measure toxins directly, and Jiang said the sequencer belongs beside them rather than in their place.

“The technology exists, and monitoring exists,” she said. “The next step is integrating rapid sequencing with established standards like cell counts and toxin measurements.”

The open question is whether species that share a site also share a trigger. The team proposed tracking which harmful algae rise together, as a first step toward a bloom forecast.

A warning that comes before a mass die-off rather than after one is the payoff that would justify the effort. For now, though, the record is two seasons of water from one lagoon, read once.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Water.

#6419. A bizarre seahorse relative found in South Australia in 2006 was actually a new genus that has never been seen since

A seahorse lookalike dredged off South Australia in 2006 belongs to a new genus known from eight specimens, none recorded in the wild since.

On February 11, 2006, a dredge working near the Gambier Islands, at the mouth of South Australia’s Spencer Gulf, brought up a small orange seahorse lookalike from about 164 feet (50 meters) down.

The dredge was sampling brachiopods, small animals with shells, for the Waterhouse Club Expedition. The club ran that survey with the South Australian Museum.

The expedition mainly targeted marine invertebrates such as sponges and soft corals. But the paper says it recorded little locality data.

It now has a name, Australyichthys aegis, and the common name helmethead sea muppet. A team led by Graham Short of the Australian Museum reports that it and two relatives are not seahorses. Also, none of the three has a verified sighting in the wild.

The paper lists eight known specimens of the genus, collected over nearly 80 years. Seven were examined for the study, at Museums Victoria, the Australian Museum, the South Australian Museum, the CSIRO fish collection and the California Academy of Sciences.

H. Howell collected the oldest in 1927, about 8 miles (13 kilometers) east of Eden in New South Wales. J.A. Tubb took one off Eden in October 1941. R.J. Slack-Smith caught another there on December 30, 1960, in a Danish seine trawl at 210 to 240 feet (64 to 73 meters).

Martin Gomon of Museums Victoria used the 1960 fish in 1997 to describe a new seahorse, Hippocampus minotaur. D. Gledhill added a male from east of Disaster Bay, south of Eden, on December 10, 1996, from 407 feet (124 meters).

On July 26, 1995, S. Hageman, P. Bock and Y. Bone collected a single female southwest of Esperance, Western Australia, at 335 feet (102 meters).

Foster and Gomon named it Hippocampus paradoxus in 2010. Ralph Foster works at the South Australian Museum, and both he and Gomon are co-authors of the new paper.

The three sites lie across more than 1,550 miles (2,500 kilometers) of coast. Trawls or dredges caught all the fish by accident, between 164 and 407 feet (50 and 124 meters) down. Since 2006, no new one has turned up.

The specimens are irreplaceable, so the team did not dissect them. Short ran the 2006 male, the 1996 Disaster Bay male and the Esperance female through a Bruker SkyScan 1173 at the Karel F. Liem BioImaging Center, at the University of Washington’s Friday Harbor Laboratories.

Each one went in wet, in a 15-milliliter plastic tube of ethanol with damp cheesecloth packed around it. The machine ran at 65 kV through a 1 mm aluminum filter. The image stacks then came out at 2,048 by 2,048 pixels.

Seahorses carry a bony crown on the head, the coronet, and plates fused into a tube around the belly. On the scans, however, Australyichthys had no coronet and no fused belly plates.

Its belly rests on three groups of small bones, front, back and middle, and the authors found that setup in no other member of the family.

In that Disaster Bay male about nine embryos showed up inside the pouch. The Esperance female had round, dense bits in its gut, probably pieces of tiny crustaceans, which is the only clue so far to what any of these fish eat.

The 2006 male was the only one of the seven kept in ethanol (the rest were fixed in formalin, which ruins DNA), and so the genetics come from that single fish.

A. King at the Australian Centre for Wildlife Genomics in Sydney took DNA from tail tissue. J. Bishop at the University of Oregon prepared the library, and an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 produced 101,723,675 reads, now filed at the U.S. National Center for Biotechnology Information as BioProject PRJNA1494570.

Susan Bassham and Clayton Small ran the comparison across 271 stretches of DNA from 23 species. The new genus sat outside the seahorses.

Instead, it fell in a group of Indo-Pacific pipefishes and pygmy pipehorses that is the seahorses’ sister group. By that result, the bent head, gripping tail and closed male pouch arose at least twice in one fish family.

That family, the Syngnathidae, is the one where males carry the eggs and give birth. It also holds tiny reef species that lost genes and changed shape to hide in coral.

The 2006 male measures 2.2 inches (56 millimeters). A photo taken when it was fresh shows an orange to pink-orange body with blotches of pink, white and pale yellow, and in ethanol it has faded to yellow-brown.

It has a very large, domed head and a row of sharp, triangular skin flaps along its back and tail. The name aegis refers to the shield of Greek mythology.

The genus name joins Latin for southern and Greek for fish, and Amanda Hay of the Australian Museum suggested calling the group “sea Muppets.”

In 2022, Long and Rodríguez proposed a cutoff for lost species. Under it, a species counts as lost after ten years with no confirmed record in the wild.

Short and his co-authors then apply that rule to the whole genus. They call Australyichthys a lost genus, a term they introduce in the paper.

The label “does not imply imminent extinction,” they wrote. Their conservation statement puts the 20-year gap down to how little anyone samples the mid-depth reefs off southern Australia.

The paper also says no one has made a targeted, non-destructive survey there. The conservation group Re:wild keeps its own list of 25 most wanted lost species.

The paper names bottom trawling as a risk for small fish that live on the seafloor. Ocean warming, lower oxygen and silt from the coast are listed too, especially for semi-enclosed waters such as Spencer Gulf.

The habitat of the 2006 fish was never recorded. The authors blame the “limited locality data recorded during this non-scientific expedition.”

Only one species has DNA, so the team placed the other two in the genus because of their bones. So far, nobody has found a female helmethead. The team did no formal IUCN Red List assessment and calls the genus data deficient.

So the paper proposes deep diving off Eden, in the Great Australian Bight and around the Gambier Islands. It also suggests eDNA tests built on the new genome.

Co-author David Harasti of the Port Stephens Fisheries Institute, who has worked on seahorse hotels in Sydney. He reported that a remotely operated vehicle has spotted pygmy seahorses in the wild.

Trawls and dredges have caught males carrying young in the austral spring and summer, so the team suggests searching then.

The Gambier Islands Group Marine Park, with no active trawling, is on its list. It lies close to where the dredge pulled up the helmethead in February 2006.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Lost Species.

#6418. A dinosaur skull, overlooked for a century, belongs to a long-clawed cousin of T. rex

A tiger-sized Isle of Wight dinosaur hunted with long claws instead of a bite; it is the first of its kind ever found in Europe.

Tyrannosaurus rex is the dinosaur most people would least want to meet. Some of its cousins hunted with long arms and curved claws instead of a crushing bite. One of them has just turned up in a museum drawer in London.

The chunk of skull had been there since 1924, and it belongs to a new species the size of a large tiger.

The new dinosaur, Invictibellatrix amberina, is the first of these clawed hunters ever found in Europe. The fossil came from a beach on the Isle of Wight, off the south coast of England. Unfortunately, that one piece of braincase is all anyone has of the dinosaur.

Cassius Morrison of UCL Earth Sciences led the study with colleagues at the Natural History Museum in London and the University of Bristol. The species belongs to a group called megaraptorans, which recent family trees put close to the tyrannosaurs or inside that family.

“It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex,” Morrison said.

“We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us,” he added. “A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small.”

The Natural History Museum bought the braincase in May 1924 from Reginald Walter Hooley, an amateur collector whose fossils came to the museum after his death.

It was picked up at the foot of a cliff at Sudmoor Point, on the island’s southwest coast. Around 120 million years ago, flash floods on a nearby floodplain piled wood and bones into debris beds. This is where the rock formed that held the new dinosaur fossil.

Those rocks, the Wessex Formation, have produced many named dinosaurs, Morrison told Earth.com. The different species did not all live side by side; the cast changed as time went on.

The surf rolled the fossil around before someone found it, wearing down its surfaces and erasing most of the skull. “It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years,” Morrison said.

In an interview with Earth.com, Morrison said the fossil came up in a search for something else.

“It was part of my Ph.D. thesis to examine if any British theropods had semi aquatic or aquatic adaptations within their skulls, especially the braincase,” he said.

Only around five theropod braincases are known from the U.K., the new one included, he added, so it had to be examined in detail.

Researchers find it difficult to place Megaraptorans because no complete skull of one has ever been found, and the best one belongs to a juvenile.

So the team scanned the fossil with X-rays at the museum and built a 3D model of the bone, plus one of the cavity that held the brain. Then they compared both with other two-legged meat-eaters.

Together, a few features set it apart from every named dinosaur on the island. An oval opening marks where the spinal cord entered the skull, and a hourglass-shaped crest runs across the back of the skull.

Furthermore, a pair of deep pits flanks the knob that joined skull to neck.

Two separate family trees, one built from 1,759 anatomical features and another from 356, both placed the fossil among the megaraptorans.

Its skull bones had fused together, which points to an adult or near-adult rather than a youngster of a known species.

Morrison said two things surprised him. The first was simply that the fossil was a megaraptoran at all. The next related to the fact that it was old, but had some relatively modern features.

“It is potentially one of the oldest, if not the oldest megaraptoran known, but had some relatively advanced features,” he told Earth.com.

Later megaraptorans grew into giants with claws up to 14 inches (35 centimeters) long. One from Argentina reached an estimated 30 to 33 feet (9 to 10 meters) and weighed as much as an elephant.

Researchers described Joaquinraptor, a megaraptoran from Patagonia, only last year.

Invictibellatrix was built on a different scale. Its braincase is about the size of one from a tyrannosaur relative that weighed 440 to 660 pounds (200 to 300 kilograms).

That makes it one of the smallest megaraptorans known, and perhaps the smallest. Judging from its closest relatives, Morrison put it at roughly 10 to 13 feet (3 to 4 meters) long and 5 feet (1.5 meters) tall.

Its claws were 4 to 8 inches long, and it would have hunted small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals, he said. “It would likely have had feathers and its claws might have been about 10cm to 20cm long,” he added.

Megaraptorans are thought to have started in Asia and ended up as top predators across the southern continents. Europe lay on the likely route, yet until now none had been found there.

“This new species is the first proof we have that megaraptorans were also present in Europe and that they reached Gondwana this way rather than island-hopping further south,” said co-author Charlie Scherer, a Ph.D. student at UCL.

The team fed the new species into a model of how the group spread. It draws on the family trees, fossil ages, and maps of the continents as they lay at the time.

In the result the team prefers, Invictibellatrix descended from an Asian population that reached Europe about 130 million years ago, and the group then moved on through Africa.

Morrison said the study adds “further evidence of a potential migration of Megaraptorans from the northern continents via Africa to the southern continents.”

By the same result, the giant southern megaraptorans arose in South America and Africa. The Australian species branched off from there. Earlier work had argued the opposite direction, starting from Australia, and Morrison’s own earlier study traced tyrannosaurs from Asia to North America.

By the Late Cretaceous, tens of millions of years later, megaraptorans had vanished from the northern continents. In contrast, their southern relatives kept growing. The authors read that absence as a regional extinction rather than a gap in the fossil record.

The authors don’t say why. Shifts in climate, changes in the environment, or competition from other predators such as tyrannosaurs are possibilities they raise.

Other animals moved between Europe and Africa at the time, spinosaurs among them.

Two caveats go with this. The two family trees disagree about where the species’ ancestors came from. The team’s preferred answer rests on the dataset with more megaraptorans in it. And the whole species is known from one worn piece of skull.

One place to look for answers is the skull itself. Braincase features make up about 4 percent of the traits in the biggest meat-eating dinosaur family trees, and the authors argue that more of them would help settle where megaraptorans belong.

“I will be greedy and say a baby megaraptoran or a relatively complete long necked sauropod,” Morrison said when asked what he would most like to find next on the Isle of Wight.

The full study was published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

#6417. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6416. A new island formed off the coast of Iceland in 1963, but very few people have ever been allowed to visit

Born from a volcanic eruption in 1963, Iceland's protected Surtsey island offers scientists a rare chance to study how life colonizes new land.

On November 14, 1963, fishermen off the south coast of Iceland noticed signs of an eruption at sea. Over the next three and a half years, the eruptions built Surtsey, a volcanic island about 20 miles (32 kilometers) from the mainland.

Iceland protected the island while it was still forming. Since then, scientists have used it as a natural laboratory to watch life arrive on brand-new land.

Going ashore without a permit is prohibited, and tourists may not land at all.

The Surtsey eruption continued until June 5, 1967, the longest continuous eruption in Iceland since the country was settled, according to the Environment Agency of Iceland.

When it ended, the island covered about 1 square mile (2.6 square kilometers) and rose 558 feet (170 meters) above sea level.

By 2006, waves, wind and rain had cut the island to about 0.54 square miles (1.4 square kilometers), and its highest point had dropped to 509 feet (155 meters).

Drill cores taken in 1979 and 2017 show pores in the island’s volcanic rock filling with new mineral cements, including a mineral called aluminous tobermorite. Marie Jackson, a research professor of geology and geophysics at the University of Utah, led that work.

“It’s not often that we have geologic processes that we can watch change at the human scale,” Jackson said in a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory feature.

In Jackson’s account, the only other places with comparable amounts of that mineral are ancient Roman harbor structures, where it formed in concrete. “Surtsey basalt is providing a geologic analogue for Roman seawater concretes,” she noted.

Surtsey became a nature reserve in 1965, while the eruption was still underway. The reserve was enlarged in 2006 and now covers about 25 square miles (65 square kilometers) of sea and island.

Visits have been restricted since 1965, mainly to prevent biological contamination. Landing on the island requires permission from the Environment Agency of Iceland.

Visitors may not disturb the island’s features, bring in organisms or soil, or leave waste. Diving near the island is not allowed.

Only one to three visits take place each year, with no more than ten to 12 visitors per trip, according to the IUCN World Heritage Outlook.

The Surtsey Research Society coordinates the research, usually with one group of about ten scientists per year. Boat trips within the reserve and viewing from the air are allowed.

Scientists have studied the island since 1964. Seeds arrived on ocean currents, and molds, bacteria and fungi appeared.

The first vascular plant appeared in 1965. It was a sea rocket, a coastal plant, found near the northern shore.

Ten vascular plant species had arrived by the end of the island’s first decade. By 2004, the count had reached 60, along with 75 bryophytes, 71 lichens and 24 fungi.

In study plots surveyed over the years, the average number of plant species rose from 4.8 in 1996 and 1997 to 10.4 in 2014 and 2015.

Scientists have also recorded 89 bird species on Surtsey, 57 of which breed elsewhere in Iceland, and 335 species of invertebrates.

A 2022 study of plant colonization on Surtsey by Sigurður H. Magnússon and colleagues at the Icelandic Institute of Natural History dates the start of a dense gull colony on the southern lava fields to 1986.

Plant colonization had been considerable from 1965 to 1979, then stalled for six years. After the gulls settled, it rose sharply, peaking in 1992 to 1995 and again in 2006 and 2007.

The authors attribute the jump to the birds bringing in more seeds and improving conditions for seedlings. Within the colony, vegetation became denser and richer in nutrients.

From 1965 to 2015, the botanists counted 74 vascular plant species on the island, 64 of them still living in 2015. The total of 74 equals about 15 percent of Iceland’s native vascular plant flora.

Even so, “most of the island still has sparse vegetation cover,” the authors write. They expect nutrients from seabirds to keep adding plant cover.

UNESCO added Surtsey to its World Heritage List in 2008. Coastal erosion is expected to remove another two-thirds of the island, leaving only its most resistant core.

The island’s measured area fell from 366 acres (148.1 hectares) in 1998 to 317 acres (128.3 hectares) in 2016.

No invasive alien species have been recorded on Surtsey so far. Invasive plants do grow on Heimaey, about 11 miles (18 kilometers) away.

The Icelandic Institute of Natural History monitors the island with the Marine Research Institute and the Agricultural University of Iceland, in cooperation with the Surtsey Research Society.

IUCN’s latest assessment of the site, finalized in October 2025, rated its conservation outlook as “Good.”

The information was obtained from UNESCO.

About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.

The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.

LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

The researchers analyzed which SARS-CoV-2 strain was associated with the most long COVID cases, controlling for patient vaccination status.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.

Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.

In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:

In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.

Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.

Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."

Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.

"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."

#6413. Mitochondria power our cells, but the ones inside parasites tell a stranger story

Mitochondria in five parasites carry dozens of protein families that people lack, which makes them candidate targets for new antiparasitic drugs.

Biology class calls mitochondria the powerhouses of the cell, but that lesson was built mostly on information from human and yeast cells, not from the cells of parasites. Across the wider tree of life, human mitochondria may, in some ways, be the exception.

A new catalog of the proteins inside mitochondria covers five single-celled parasites and the cells of one plant. It turned up dozens of protein families that the parasites share but people lack entirely.

Because these parasites tend to depend on their mitochondria to survive, those missing-in-humans proteins are now candidates for new antiparasitic drugs.

The researchers belong to the MitoCarta Tree of Life consortium, led by Vamsi Mootha of the Broad Institute. He is also a professor of systems biology at Harvard Medical School. Michael Chen, a Harvard M.D.-Ph.D. student, led the comparison.

What the study produced is a list of candidates, not any tested treatments.

About 2 billion years ago, a host cell swallowed a bacterium but didn’t break down its molecules. That bacterium’s descendants became mitochondria.

Over time most of its genes moved into the host’s nucleus, leaving only a small stretch of mitochondrial DNA behind. Today almost every protein inside a mitochondrion is made outside it and imported.

Researchers call that full set of proteins the mitoproteome. Versions already existed for humans and yeast.

The consortium added the plant Arabidopsis and five parasites, among them Giardia, which causes diarrhea, and Acanthamoeba, which can infect the eyes of contact lens wearers. Together, those five parasites cause an estimated 1 billion infections a year.

Across all eight organisms, the team counted 8,619 mitochondrial proteins. The sizes varied wildly. Giardia‘s mitochondria held 59 proteins, while the parasite Trypanosoma held 1,666, nearly half again as many as found in mitochondria of a human cell.

So there’s no single standard version of a mitochondrion. The team sorted the proteins into 3,199 families. Of those, 43 percent carried no feature linking them to any well-studied protein. That suggests mitochondria still hold plenty of unstudied biology.

Giardia‘s mitochondria have shrunk so far that they no longer make energy. The only job anyone knew they did was building iron-sulfur clusters, tiny bundles of iron and sulfur atoms that many proteins need in order to work.

In an interview with Earth.com, Mootha said the team chose Giardia because its mitochondria were already known to be among the simplest.

“Indeed, its mitoproteome proved to be very small – but excitingly, one-half of its proteins are of unknown function.”

Some relatives go further. The team’s computer predictions found only 23 likely mitochondrial proteins in Monocercomonoides exilis, a distant single-celled relative reported to have lost the organelle entirely.

Another, Skoliomonas litria, was also thought to have lost its mitochondria, but the team found signature mitochondrial parts in it, which raises the possibility that a tiny remnant survives.

Mitochondria are already a target for some antiparasitic drugs. Atovaquone, used against malaria parasites and Babesia, targets a mitochondrial protein that humans also carry. And drug resistance to these established medicines is emerging.

So Chen’s team looked for proteins that at least two kinds of parasites keep in their mitochondria and humans don’t make at all. They found 33. Two of them, enzymes called NDH2 and class I fumarate hydratase, have already been studied by other groups as drug targets.

Three of the 33, class I fumarate hydratase among them, do the same jobs as human enzymes while sharing no resemblance to them. In principle, a drug aimed at the parasite version could leave the human version alone.

The team also checked a malaria parasite. Seventeen of the candidates have a counterpart in Plasmodium knowlesi, and a recent gene-knockout screen found 13 of those 17 were essential to its survival.

Biologists call single-celled organisms like these protists, and a drug that worked against several of them at once would be a pan-parasite drug.

“As mitochondria tend to be essential for pathogenic protists, these proteins may represent promising ‘pan-parasite’ drug targets for neglected tropical diseases,” Mootha told Earth.com.

The team then trained an AI program on the new protein lists and used it to predict the mitochondria of roughly two hundred species.

With those predictions, the team worked backward to the last common ancestor of all complex cells, which lived roughly 1.5 to 2 billion years ago.

The team estimated that the ancestor had about 1,438 mitochondrial proteins, with a wide margin of error.

By their math, about 70 percent of human mitochondrial proteins trace back to this ancestor, compared with 14 to 16 percent in earlier attempts. By that estimate, most parts of our own mitochondria are very old.

Most of the ancestor’s protein families show up today mainly in microbes that use oxygen. But about 15 percent are linked to microbes that live without it, including enzymes that make hydrogen gas.

Acanthamoeba still has both abilities. Without oxygen, mitochondria purified from the amoeba produce hydrogen gas. The team concluded that the ancestor’s mitochondria may have been able to work with oxygen or without it.

Human mitochondria lack dozens of proteins that the ancestor had and many other species kept. Mootha said the textbook picture comes largely from mammal and yeast cells.

“In some instances, our mitochondria appear to be the odd ones,” he added.

Scientists have long debated whether mitochondria arrived early or late in the making of complex cells. So the team estimated when each ancient protein arrived, using the length of branches on protein family trees.

Proteins inherited from the host cell, a relative of today’s Asgard archaea, came in early. Mitochondrial proteins came in later on average, after the nucleus, the internal skeleton and other cell parts were already in place.

That supports what researchers call the mito-late view, which earlier studies had also backed. Peroxisomes, another kind of compartment inside the cell, appear to have arrived around the same time.

The ancient proteins matter for medicine, too. Of 266 genes tied to mitochondrial diseases in people, the team traced 240 back to that ancestor.

The authors list several limits. Sequenced genomes still favor well-studied groups of organisms, and some protein families that look unique to one group may have distant relatives that current tools can’t detect.

Reconstructing cells from well over a billion years ago is also hard. The authors said the limits of current methods may affect how accurate the ancestral reconstruction is.

For drugs, a missing-in-humans protein is only the first filter. Mootha said the next steps are to learn more about the pathways these proteins work in and whether the parasites need them at every stage of life. Researchers also have to judge whether each protein can be blocked by a drug at all.

“Then once candidate targets are identified, there is a long path for drug discovery and development and testing,” he said.

The team’s data are public, so other labs can take up that work. The next question is whether blocking any one of the 33 candidates can stop a parasite without harming the person it infects.

The full study was published in the journal Cell.

#6411. Hospital visits for heart failure and heart attacks rose faster when states legalized recreational cannabis

After recreational cannabis legalization, hospital stays for heart failure, heart attack and atrial fibrillation rose 2% to 4% a year faster.

Voting to legalize recreational cannabis feels like a decision about the people who choose to use it. The hospitals in a state get a vote too, in the form of who shows up at the door.

Legal sales began in the western United States in 2014. After that, hospital stays for heart failure, heart attack, and a common irregular heartbeat climbed faster there than in the rest of the country. The gap was 2% to 4% a year for each diagnosis. It did not appear for conditions cannabis has no known link to.

Samuel Slavin, a cardiologist at Boston University’s Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine, led the analysis of more than 50 million hospital records with colleagues at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. His team can’t say cannabis caused any one of those stays.

In an interview with Earth.com, Slavin was careful about what the numbers mean. “This is a modest relative increase. For any one person, the associated risk is likely small. But across millions of people, even small shifts can mean a large number of additional hospital visits,” he said.

The team tracked six diagnoses, and three of them climbed faster in the West after legal sales began. Hospital stays for atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat, rose 2.3% a year faster than in other regions. Heart attacks rose 3.1% faster, and heart failure 3.7% faster.

The gaps are yearly, so they stack. After five years of legal sales, heart failure admissions in the West would sit roughly a fifth above what the rest of the country’s trend would predict.

Stroke and dangerous clots in the veins trended upward too, as did a fast rhythm from the heart’s lower chambers. The amounts were small enough that chance could explain them.

The West had started out healthier on every count. Before legalization, it recorded about 206 heart failure stays per 100,000 people a year, against 333 elsewhere.

The records came from the National Inpatient Sample, a federal database that collects one in five hospital discharges from states covering about 97% of Americans. Slavin’s team pulled 50,042,564 of them, from 2012 through 2018.

Colorado opened the first legal recreational shops in January 2014, and Washington followed that July. One more western state joined each year after that.

By the end of the study, nearly everyone in the Census Bureau’s Western region lived in a state with legal sales or next door to one.

Outside the West, no shop opened until Massachusetts in late November 2018, too late to matter. That timing made the comparison possible.

So the team compared the West’s trend before and after legalization with the trend everywhere else, a standard way to judge a policy. They adjusted for patients’ age, sex, race, and ZIP code income, and checked that the two regions had been moving in parallel before the first shop opened.

Two checks guard the result. Hospital stays coded as cannabis-related rose 13.6% a year faster in the West, so the method could see legalization at all. Stays for urinary stones and opioid problems, which cannabis is not thought to affect, did not budge.

Cannabis has a plausible route to the heart. THC, its main active compound, speeds the heart rate and raises blood pressure, and it may make blood more likely to clot.

Earlier studies had linked use to arrhythmias and heart attacks, though others found nothing. All of them, the authors wrote, struggled to separate cannabis from the pain, anxiety, or other drugs that often come with it.

Comparing regions rather than people sidesteps that problem, and legalization is also tied to more use among older adults, who already carry the most heart risk.

One earlier study of the same kind found cardiac deaths rose 1.3% to 2.3% after states passed medical cannabis laws. The authors read the two results as pointing the same way.

Slavin kept the result in proportion. “I think these findings matter more for policymakers than for someone deciding whether to visit a local dispensary,” he said.

States, Slavin added, should treat legalization with the same care as a new drug, and could build heart data collection into the policy from the start.

The hospital database only allows comparisons between census regions, so the whole West counted as legal from the start even though most of its states joined later. That would tend to shrink the gap, not inflate it.

The records also can’t say whether patients smoked cannabis or ate it, whether illegal use changed, or whether some other western trend began the same year by coincidence. And the records stop in 2018, before the legal market had matured.

Legalization changes many things at once, Slavin told Earth.com, including how many people use cannabis, how often, which products they choose, and how they interact with the health system. The study, he said, looks at whole populations and can’t show that cannabis caused any particular heart problem.

Whether the risk comes from smoke, from THC, or from something else is the question the team can’t answer yet. Slavin said those answers matter because they would tell people which products and ways of using carry more or less risk.

Two routes could get there. Sales records could show whether edibles and inhaled products differ in their effects, the authors wrote. And states still weighing legalization, Slavin said, could roll it out in staggered, randomized steps and collect heart data as they go.

Slavin also said cannabis’s Schedule I status, the most restrictive federal category, makes it harder to study. In his view, the findings strengthen the case for moving it to a less restrictive one.

For now, his advice is narrow. “People who use cannabis – especially those with existing heart conditions or risk factors – may want to talk with their doctor,” he said.

The full study was published in the journal BMJ Open.

#6410. A new telescope in Chile found two more stable Neptune trojans in just its first three weeks

Rubin Observatory's test survey spotted 2025 MH348 and 2025 NN80, doubling the known stable Neptune trojans in the trailing cloud from two to four.

On June 21, 2025, the camera of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory picked up two faint moving objects. A new test survey on Cerro Pachón in Chile had begun just one day earlier.

One of them got the designation 2025 MH348. It orbits the Sun at about 30 times Earth’s distance. It also belongs to the trailing group of Neptune trojans, small icy bodies that ride behind the planet.

Meg Schwamb of Queen’s University Belfast and 14 co-authors now report two confirmed members of that group and one candidate.

Before this, only two long-lived trailing trojans were on the books. Still, the team says its sample is too small to estimate how many exist.

Neptune trojans move on Neptune’s orbit in two swarms. One sits about 60 degrees ahead of the planet, at a Lagrange point called L4, and the other sits 60 degrees behind it, at L5.

By the time the authors wrote the paper, surveys had found over 30 Neptune trojans. However, most of what astronomers know about them comes from L4.

Seen from Earth, L5 sat on or close to the Galactic center for more than 15 years. Fields less than 10 degrees from the Galactic plane teem with stars. The paper says that high stellar density “significantly hindered” the discovery of trailing trojans.

By 2025 a large swath of the L5 cloud had come out of the Galactic plane. Then Rubin’s test fields covered part of it by chance, even though their designers had not aimed them at Neptune trojans.

According to the paper, trojans on orbits stable for billions of years are primordial, not recent arrivals. So their sizes, colors, spin rates and orbits carry information about the disk of planetesimals Neptune migrated through.

For every known Neptune trojan, the Minor Planet Center lists about 450 trojans of Jupiter, even though earlier surveys estimate the Neptune population is 4 to 10 times larger.

Rubin’s Science Validation survey started on June 20, 2025. It took 30-second exposures in six filters and imaged its fields every night, instead of every three or four nights as in the main survey, and covered about 3,000 square degrees near the ecliptic over the commissioning window.

The Simonyi Survey Telescope has an 8.4-meter (27.6-foot) mirror and a 3.2-gigapixel camera with a 9.6-square-degree field of view. The authors wrote that this makes Rubin “an ideal discovery machine” for the region.

2025 MH348 and the candidate 2025 MD138 turned up on UT June 21, 2025, and 2025 NN80 on UT July 7.

The searches used Rubin’s Solar System Processing pipeline with two codes, an expanded version of HelioLinC and a newer program called pointdexter, developed by Matt Holman and Kevin Napier to look for distant moving objects.

The detections were reported to the Minor Planet Center in February 2026. Users of the Minor Planet Mailing List, an online group of amateur and professional asteroid observers, then flagged the three as possible L5 trojans, and the paper credits those discussions with helping inspire the work.

Afterward, astronomers linked older detections by the Pan-STARRS1 telescope in Hawaii to 2025 MH348 and 2025 NN80. That allowed orbit fits over several oppositions. The data arc for 2025 MH348 grew to 2,595 days and for 2025 NN80 to 1,547 days.

The team took orbits from NASA JPL’s Small-Body Database, dated June 5, 2026. It ran them in the Small Body Dynamics Tool, with the Sun and the four giant planets pulling on each object.

For each body it also drew 100 clones from the JPL covariance matrix, which gives orbits nudged within the measurement errors, and ran high-resolution 10-million-year integrations before extending them to 1 billion years.

All 100 clones of 2025 MH348 and all 100 of 2025 NN80 were still in step with Neptune at 1 billion years. JPL lists their orbital periods at about 164 years, the same as Neptune’s.

The two older stable L5 trojans are 2008 LC18 and 2011 HM102. Scott Sheppard and Chad Trujillo reported 2008 LC18 in 2010. With the Rubin pair added, the list of trailing trojans on gigayear-stable orbits has four names.

Each of the four has an inclination above 25 degrees (28.7 and 29.7 degrees for the new pair), which fits earlier models in which trojan stability peaks near 30 degrees and again below 10 degrees.

Rubin measured the objects in the g, r, i and z filters. 2025 NN80 had 32 measurements, 2025 MH348 had 11 and 2025 MD138 had 15.

The new three are bluer than the two L5 trojans measured in a 2023 study. Put together with the earlier pair, the L5 colors fall in the same locus as the L4 swarm. The authors take that as further support for a single parent population.

A spectrum-reconstruction model matched all three to a water-ice spectral type that is common among Neptune trojans. The paper calls this a probabilistic assignment and says it does not replace near-infrared spectra.

Co-authors work in São Paulo, Tucson, Seattle, Ann Arbor and Belfast. The authors thank Breakthrough Listen and Queen’s University Belfast for supporting the LSST solar system First Data Sprint.

2025 MD138 remains a candidate because its 38 days of Rubin observations leave large error bars on its distance and orbit shape.

Its best-fit orbit stays stable for a billion years. Of its 100 clones, 36 behaved like trojans over 10 million years and 23 lasted to 1 billion.

Its inclination is about 6 degrees, and all 23 surviving clones kept that low tilt. If follow-up confirms it, it would be the first known long-lived L5 trojan on a low-tilt orbit.

There is no population estimate in the paper either. Rubin has not yet published how efficient its early moving-object search was. So the authors did not compare their haul with predicted numbers.

Rubin started its 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time at the end of June 2026. Rain and snow on Cerro Pachón halted it in mid-July. Science work was due to resume in early southern spring, after a planned engineering shutdown.

The observatory released its first images of the sky in June 2025, and by April 2026 its early data had produced more than 11,000 newly discovered asteroids. The decade-long survey of the southern sky covers nearly all the area where L5 trojans should be.

Co-author Joseph Murtagh, of the University of Washington, led a 2026 study. It predicts that the survey will quadruple the known Neptune trojans. It expects tens to hundreds in the trailing swarm, most of them in the first two years.

Other bodies have been found moving in step with Neptune farther out, and a second trojan sharing Earth’s orbit was confirmed in 2022.

The authors describe the three objects as “the tip of the iceberg” for the Neptune trojan science Rubin will enable. Sixteen years after astronomers reported the first L5 trojan, the count of long-lived ones stands at four. Two of them came from Rubin’s first weeks of testing.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

#6409. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6408. Bandicoot snouts reveal an evolutionary puzzle hiding in plain sight

Bandicoot skulls vary with climate and location, with climate explaining more shape differences than body size alone does.

Most bandicoots and bilbies find their food the same way: by scratching and digging through soil.

Their snouts, however, look very different from one species to the next. Some are short and sturdy, while others are long and narrow.

A new study of museum skulls found that climate and location help explain those differences, and that body size alone does not.

The researchers concluded that skull shape, more than size, is where these small to medium-sized marsupials changed most as they spread across Australia and New Guinea.

The work was led by Dr. Meg Martin and colleagues in Professor Natalie Warburton’s research group at Murdoch University’s Harry Butler Institute.

The team collaborated with Dr. Kenny Travouillon of the Western Australian Museum.

The researchers worked only with skulls, so no living animals were observed digging.

“When people think of bandicoots, they often picture a fairly similar group of small, digging marsupials,” Warburton said.

“But when we compared their skulls in three dimensions, we found remarkable differences, particularly in the length and shape of their snouts.”

The researchers scanned 127 adult skulls from 25 species, most of them from the museum’s mammal collection. Three of the species are extinct.

Teeth are shiny, so to cut down on reflections, each skull was first coated with a thin white layer of magnesium oxide. The coating was made by burning strips of magnesium in a fume hood.

Each skull was then scanned in two positions on a rotating platform, and the scans were combined into a single 3D model.

The researchers marked the same 54 points on every model, such as the seams where skull bones meet and spots on certain teeth.

They left out the cheekbones and a few other areas, because those parts were often damaged or worn on old museum specimens and fossils.

Comparing the 54 points across skulls allowed the team to measure shape separately from size.

That step matters, because a bigger animal can have a differently shaped head partly because it’s bigger. Warburton said a single skull can tell researchers a lot about an animal.

“Its shape is influenced by ancestry, feeding, sensory systems, and the mechanical demands placed on the head, so comparing skulls across species gives us another way of understanding how animals have adapted over evolutionary time,” she said.

The biggest difference was between short, broad skulls with wide braincases and long, slender skulls with narrow faces.

Short-nosed bandicoots, including the quenda of south-western Australia, had the short, sturdy type, and the smallest of these bandicoots had the most extreme versions.

A group of bandicoots called Perameles had longer snouts and narrower skulls, while the New Guinea species were in between.

Of the two bilby species measured, one had a skull close to the average for the whole group, and the other was more like Perameles.

Closely related bandicoots also tended to have similar skulls.

Knowing a skull’s genus, a group of closely related species, explained about 55% of the differences in shape, while knowing its exact species explained about 75%.

So why would close relatives end up with such different faces? Warburton pointed to the way each animal finds its food.

“For animals that spend a lot of their time searching and digging for food, the snout is an important part of how they interact with their environment,” she said.

“A long, narrow snout may help an animal probe through soil and fallen leaves for food, while a shorter, stronger snout may be better suited to digging.”

That idea fits what is known about other mammals. Long, thin snouts often belong to animals that pick small, scattered bits of food out of soil or leaf litter, and anteaters and echidnas are well-known examples.

Diet may matter too. Short-nosed bandicoots eat tubers and other underground plant parts, which can be tougher to chew than many insects.

New Guinea’s bandicoots, by contrast, appear to eat a lot of fungi and soft-bodied invertebrates from the forest floor.

The researchers suggest that tougher food, or deeper and more forceful digging, may help explain why short-nosed bandicoots have sturdier skulls.

Still, most bandicoots eat a wide mix of foods, and many species have little detailed diet information, so the team didn’t treat skull shape as a direct guide to diet.

To test the role of climate, the team looked up climate data for the place where each skull was collected, using a global database called WorldClim.

They kept six measures of temperature and rainfall that didn’t overlap much.

Together, climate, location and body size accounted for about 35% of the differences in skull shape. Climate on its own explained about 13%, nearly twice as much as size on its own.

That makes climate the bigger factor of the two, although most of the differences in skull shape remain unexplained.

The single strongest link was with latitude, meaning how far north or south a skull was collected.

Among the climate measures, rainfall in the driest month of the year had the strongest link.

Other studies of rodents and of carnivores in the dog and cat families have also linked skull shape to climate.

Size still played a part, but after the team removed its effect, the groups still differed clearly in shape. Males had bigger skulls than females, yet their skull shapes didn’t differ reliably.

These results point to links rather than causes, so they can’t tell how climate affected the skulls.

Bandicoot fossils go back about 26 million years, and although the record is patchy, it includes skull shapes no living species has.

The extinct pig-footed bandicoots, which ate mostly plants, had an unusually broad back to the roof of the mouth.

Partial skulls from the Riversleigh fossil sites in Queensland couldn’t be measured, but their features were compared.

Some early bandicoots were tiny, weighing about 3.5 to 5.3 ounces (100 to 150 grams), with snouts shorter than any living bandicoot’s.

Their skulls look like those of antechinuses, small marsupials from a different family, which suggests these early bandicoots ate insects.

Long snouts appear later, in a fossil species called Madju variae. Its place on the family tree suggests long snouts evolved before the modern bandicoot families split apart.

The tiny insect-eaters and some larger meat-eating bandicoots died out as Australia was becoming drier and its climate less stable.

Most survivors were omnivores, and the researchers suggest that eating many kinds of food mattered more than specializing.

Short-nosed bandicoots later evolved shorter snouts again. In this group, the earliest branch has the longest snout and a later branch the shortest, a sign of a fairly recent change.

For 13 of the 25 species, the team had only three skulls or fewer.

Many fossil species couldn’t be measured at all, so bandicoot skulls were probably even more varied than this study could capture.

The rest of the skeleton is also a gap. The researchers wrote that it’s still poorly understood how the body below the head contributes to digging.

Future studies of the whole skeleton, along with Riversleigh fossils that haven’t been described yet, could help show how extinction and climate change shaped the bandicoots living today.

The full study was published in the Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society.
