Live Science readers respond to a recent poll about whether they'd visit the Red Planet even with potential health risks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For centuries, Mars has been seen as a potential place for future human settlements. But long-duration space travel comes with serious risks to astronauts' health, including those resulting from cosmic radiation and the effects of microgravity.

A new study found that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what astronauts might encounter during a Mars mission developed more scar tissue around their hearts' small blood vessels compared with a control group. Although the findings haven't been validated in humans, the results contribute to growing concerns about the potential effects of long-haul space missions on astronauts' health.

Given these new findings, Live Science asked its readers whether they'd travel to the Red Planet, despite these potential health risks. Over 240 readers weighed in, with 65% picking "No, I don't think the risks are worth it."

Interestingly enough, the comments reflect a slightly different trend. One reader wrote, "Any pioneers who travel to Mars will be facing the prospect of death and never coming back. Even if they make it back, there are any number of health issues that could come up. These risks have not stopped people from exploring throughout human history. The bigger question is who to send?"

Other commenters echoed this sentiment, with another reader posting, "Explorers in the past have always been exposed to unusual risks; without the risk takers we would still believe the world is flat."

Beyond the feelings that Mars will be explored anyway, despite the health risks, other commenters highlighted the cost of these missions, with one reader stating, "Sending flesh water balloons to Mars is ridiculous. For the cost of one human on Mars, we could literally probe the entire solar system and map/sample/rove every planet and every major Moon."

Others highlighted the mental and emotional cost of a trip to Mars. "As a devoted sci-fi fan for decades, I always wished I could go into space," another reader noted. "Now that I am 77 years old, I realize I would miss the outdoors. The wind and trees, the birdsong and sweet grass under my feet would be a devastating loss. Let the brave explorers go instead. Life is too brief to leave this planet for the uncertainty and dangers of space travel."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know your thoughts in the comments!

#6405. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 7: Venus meets the Moon

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Venus is already primed to capture attention above the eastern horizon before sunrise. This morning, the Moon passes 1.1° due south of Earth’s sister planet at 7 A.M. EST.

You can easily catch the pair an hour before sunrise, some 6° high in the east and climbing as the sky begins to brighten. Magnitude –4.5 Venus blazes to the upper left of the delicate crescent Moon, whose western limb is just barely lit as the Sun sets across the lunar nearside. Look for earthshine on the already-shadowed portion of Luna’s face, as sunlight bouncing off Earth lights it up.

Near Venus is another bright light: This is Spica, Virgo’s alpha star, shining at magnitude 1.0 and also lingering in the morning twilight. This morning it lies 1.3° northeast of Venus, with the planet and star roughly side by side above the horizon. Use this view as an anchor point: By the 10th, Venus will have moved to stand due west of this star and will be located to its upper right.

#6403. Tropical forests are changing in profound ways that are overlooked when simply studying average temperatures

Decades of weather records reveal more extreme heat in two tropical forests, while rainfall patterns are shifting in different directions.

Tropical rainforests experience relatively little temperature variation through the year.

At two well-studied forests in the Caribbean basin, the average temperature has risen only slowly over the past few decades.

The hottest days, though, have become far more common, and the rain has turned more extreme in a different way at each site.

The plants and animals in these forests are adapted to steady temperatures, the researchers wrote.

So a jump in extreme heat can matter even when the averages hardly move, and at these two forests, the extremes are where the change showed up most clearly.

Alonso Ramírez, a professor in the Department of Applied Ecology at North Carolina State University, led the work. He has a long history with both forests.

Ramírez worked as a field technician at one of the forests before graduate school, and he directed the other for 15 years.

The team pulled decades of daily weather records from two stations. The La Selva Research Station is in a lowland rainforest in Costa Rica.

The El Verde Field Station is a mountain forest site in Puerto Rico and the main base of the Luquillo Long-Term Ecological Research program.

Temperature records ran from 1992 at La Selva and from 2000 at El Verde, and the rain records went back even further.

The average day is about 77°F (25.1°C) at La Selva and about 74°F (23.6°C) at El Verde.

At both sites, the gap between the coolest month and the warmest is less than about 7°F (4°C). In other words, temperatures vary little between seasons.

To find extreme heat, the researchers ranked every day on record at each site and flagged the hottest 5% as hot days.

“In La Selva prior to 2024, you had an average of eight hot days – days where the temperature exceeded the 95th percentile of temperatures at that site – per year,” Ramírez said.

“Now that number is up to 30. These spikes in temperature are becoming more severe and more common.”

El Verde had the same rise. The team got the same result with stricter cutoffs, the hottest 3% and the hottest 1% of days. The hot days themselves also got hotter over time.

Much of the jump came from 2023 and 2024, when temperatures ran high at both forests.

The team estimated that average temperatures at both sites rose by about 0.52°F (0.29°C) per decade.

That’s close to the warming earlier studies have reported across the wider Caribbean.

That estimate depends heavily on the regional figure the researchers gave their model as a starting point, as the authors made clear.

A rise in hot days, they wrote, may not be visible in average temperature records at all.

Total annual rainfall showed no significant trend at either site.

Both forests are very wet, with La Selva averaging about 164 inches (4,166 millimeters) a year and El Verde about 143 inches (3,636 millimeters).

At La Selva, days with more than about 3.7 inches (93 millimeters) of rain rose from around one a year in 1983 through 1985 to six in 2024. Days with no rain at all dropped from 128 in 1983 to 70 in 2024.

More frequent heavy downpours can disturb a forest even when the yearly total stays the same, the authors wrote.

El Verde moved the other way. Its count of heavy rainfall days didn’t change. But days with almost no rain, less than about a twentieth of an inch (1.4 millimeters), rose from 152 to 170 a year.

Marcelo Ardón, a co-author of the study, is a professor in the Department of Forestry and Environmental Resources and the Center for Geospatial Analytics at NC State.

“That was surprising, that one is getting wetter and one is getting drier,” Ardón said.

“Given how close they are to each other, we expected to find similar trends across the two sites. This shows how climate change is happening right now, and we can demonstrate that with data that doesn’t stretch that far back.”

The researchers wrote that the El Verde result supports projections of a drier Caribbean, including Puerto Rico.

Rainforests are adapted to steady rain, they added, and are especially vulnerable to drought.

The team also checked small forest streams. Water in a La Selva stream warmed by about 0.4°F (0.2°C) between 2007 and 2024.

A stream at El Verde warmed by about 1.6°F (0.9°C) between 2006 and 2024.

The La Selva stream is fed partly by groundwater estimated at about 2,500 years old, which the authors suggested may help explain its smaller rise.

The El Verde stream depends less on groundwater and runs through a forest that hurricanes often damage.

Earlier field and lab studies suggest that even small changes in water temperature can change which insects live in a stream and how fast their young develop.

At La Selva, rising temperatures have already been linked to lower forest productivity and to a drop in the number of insect species.

“A lot of people tend to think of the tropics as being stable and unchanging, especially in protected areas like the ones we’re studying,” said Ramírez.

“Conventional wisdom would say that these places should not show much of a change from anthropogenic impacts,” he added.

“Instead, these two sites that are hotspots for research are showing clear changes in climate and in the environment, which then affects the functioning of the ecosystem.”

Two forests are a small sample of a big region. The authors see La Selva and El Verde as typical of Caribbean settings, so similar shifts may be happening across the region, but that hasn’t been tested.

Streams at both sites also spent more time at high water, with the yearly hours at those levels roughly doubling.

The statistics behind that trend were weak, so it’s possible the pattern came up by chance.

The researchers haven’t yet checked whether the warmer temperatures and changing rainfall patterns are changing life in these streams.

The next step is to find out whether the insects and other animals in the streams at both forests are already responding.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Climate.

#6402. Researchers warn that warmer weather is helping mosquitoes spread dangerous diseases like malaria and dengue

A century of data shows bed nets, drugs and growing cities explain much of why malaria and dengue went separate ways as the planet warmed.

Scientists have long predicted that a warmer world would bring more disease from mosquitoes, and dengue has kept rising along with the heat. Malaria went the other way.

Over a century of increasing temperatures, the area where malaria was a constant presence shrank to about half of what it had been, while dengue infections climbed to record highs.

According to a new review of the evidence, much of that split comes from outside the weather. People pushed malaria back with decades of bed nets, spraying, and drugs, while the growth of cities favored the mosquitoes that carry dengue.

Toby Cumming, a research fellow at the Health and Climate Initiative in Monash University’s School of Public Health, led the work with three colleagues. It is a review of studies that other teams have already published, not a new experiment.

In an interview with Earth.com, Cumming said the climate in many parts of the world is becoming more suitable for diseases spread by mosquitoes. “We cannot draw a straight line from climate suitability to rates of malaria and dengue transmission,” Cumming added.

Both diseases reach people through a bite. Malaria comes from a parasite carried by Anopheles mosquitoes, which bite mostly at night. Dengue comes from a virus carried by Aedes mosquitoes, which bite during the day.

Mosquitoes are cold-blooded, so their body temperature follows the air around them. At 59°F (15°C), a young Aedes aegypti takes 40 days to become an adult. At 95°F (35°C), it takes seven.

Warmth also makes mosquitoes bite more often. It also shortens the time the parasite or virus needs to develop inside the insect before it can infect a person.

There’s a ceiling, though. Past a certain point, heat starts to hurt the mosquito. Models suggest malaria spreads best at about 77°F to 82°F (25°C to 28°C). For dengue, it’s about 79°F to 84°F (26°C to 29°C).

Rain works in both directions. Heavy downpours can wash eggs and larvae away, while drought can leave stagnant pools in riverbeds and push families to store water in open containers near their homes.

Asked how people can protect themselves from dengue, Cumming said the best thing is to avoid bites, with long, loose clothing and insect repellent. Emptying containers that hold water around the home helps too.

The authors put numbers on how much warming has already shifted the odds. Between the 1950s and the decade ending in 2024, the climate’s estimated potential to spread dengue rose 12 percent for Aedes aegypti and 49 percent for its cousin, Aedes albopictus.

Over the same stretch, the area where the climate suits malaria grew by only about 2 percent. In Africa, the malaria map is moving.

One analysis cited in the review found that the elevation limit of malaria mosquitoes rose about 21 feet (6.5 meters) a year from 1898 to 2016.

Even so, the authors call the evidence for climate-driven shifts in malaria more contested than for dengue.

Dengue’s spread is easier to see. The disease has spread locally in places where it hadn’t before, including the southern United States, and it’s showing up more often in mainland France. Earth.com has also reported on rising dengue risk in California.

More than 14 million dengue cases were reported to the World Health Organization in 2024. That was more than double the previous annual record.

The longest view comes from a 2010 analysis in the journal Nature. Around 1900, malaria was a constant presence across an estimated 58 percent of the world’s land. By 2007, that figure had fallen to 30 percent.

Within the smaller area, far fewer people carried the parasite. In Africa, the share of people infected with the deadliest malaria parasite fell from 40 percent in 1900 to 1929, to 24 percent in 2010 to 2015.

Europe shows the same pattern. Malaria began to fade there in the 1800s while temperatures were rising, and the review credits better living conditions, better health care, and improved irrigation and drainage.

Cold didn’t stop the disease, either. Malaria was common in the marshy parishes of England from the 16th to the 18th centuries, during an especially cold period. In Finland, mosquitoes survived freezing winters by sheltering inside houses and stables.

The two diseases differ first in the tools people built to fight them. Efforts to wipe out malaria go back to the 1950s, with house spraying and mass drug campaigns, and later with bed nets treated with insecticide.

Global spending on malaria rose from $1.5 billion to $4.3 billion between 2000 and 2016. Over that time, the yearly rate of new cases fell 36 percent and the death rate fell 60 percent.

“What started as a climate story – the impact of temperature, rainfall and humidity on malaria and dengue – became a human story,” Cumming told Earth.com.

Dengue had no matching toolkit. There are still no drugs that treat the virus, vaccines are only now arriving, and bed nets do little against mosquitoes that bite in daylight.

And mosquitoes are building resistance to insecticides, a problem the authors flag for both diseases.

Cities are the second difference. Aedes mosquitoes lay eggs in gutters and water containers, and cities offer plenty of those, along with lots of people to bite.

Anopheles prefer more natural pools, which cities tend to lack, so urban growth tends to cut malaria.

The authors flag one important exception. Anopheles stephensi, a malaria mosquito from Asia that breeds in artificial containers, has now settled into cities in the Horn of Africa.

The good news on malaria has slowed. New cases per 1,000 people at risk fell from 79 in 2000 to 59 in 2015. By 2024, the figure was back up to 64.

In 18 countries, the rate rose by at least 70 percent between 2015 and 2024. Resistance to key malaria drugs is a growing concern too.

Extreme weather can undo progress quickly. After record flooding hit Pakistan in 2022, malaria cases there rose fivefold.

Asked what should be done first to curb the spread, Cumming said the answer is a renewed commitment from the global community to fight malaria and dengue.

That includes scaling up public health measures that work and speeding up research on new ways to prevent and treat both diseases.

The forecasts don’t agree on malaria. Some models predict it will spread into new areas as the planet warms. Others predict that hotter, drier conditions will shrink it in parts of Africa where it’s common today.

Adding wealth to a model changes the picture. Using climate alone, one model estimated that 5.2 billion people would be at risk of malaria by 2050. When it also counted each country’s economic output per person, the estimate dropped to 2.0 billion.

Much of the temperature evidence also comes from lab studies that were never checked in the field. And mosquitoes may adapt to local heat, which fixed temperature rules can’t capture.

For dengue, newer tools are arriving. One vaccine has been licensed in many countries since 2022. The World Mosquito Program, a not-for-profit group owned by Monash University, releases mosquitoes carrying a bacterium called Wolbachia, which makes them less able to spread the virus.

It’s still unclear whether those tools can do for dengue what bed nets and drugs did for malaria. In order to find out, researchers will need years of dengue case records from the places that use them.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6401. Nov. 7, 1882: A Great Comet transforms astrophotography

In early September 1882, a comet was sighted from the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa. The comet brightened over the following weeks, reaching a magnitude of -2 on the 15th; at perihelion two days later, it was bright enough to be visible during the day. But at the time, David Gill, the director of the Cape Observatory, was busy observing minor planets Victoria and Sappho. It wasn’t until Oct. 12 that, his minor planet observations completed, he turned his attention to the comet and began photographing it.

Gill captured images of the Great Comet of 1882 on Oct. 12, 20, and 21, and Nov. 7, 13, and 14. The Nov. 7 shot was the one he would become famous for, though: It was not the first photograph of a comet, but rather would signal a change in astronomers’ uses of astrophotography. The photo was a 100-minute exposure, resulting an image that included stars to 10th magnitude and the comet’s 18-degree tail. Spurred by the large number of stars captured in his photo, Gill saw the potential for using astrophotography for star mapping and began the Cape Photographic Durchmusterung. (Durchmusterung means “close examination” or “scrutiny.”) The project would catalog nearly a half-million southern stars. Gill shared the successes of the program internationally, prompting the assembly of the world’s first major astronomical conference. As a result, astronomers worldwide began to move away from traditional, manual star mapping and towards more efficient and comprehensive photographic techniques.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6399. What happens when engineers grind up eggshells and squeeze them into a lightweight metal?

Eggshell powder pressed into magnesium bonded to the metal and made tiny samples tougher to crush.

Most eggshells end up in the trash or the compost bin. Yet a shell is almost pure calcium carbonate, the same calcium compound that metal makers normally get from mined rock.

Engineers have now packed ground-up kitchen eggshells into a block of magnesium metal and pressed it through a spinning die. The shell powder spread evenly through the metal.

Part of it also reacted with the magnesium around it, which bonded shell to metal chemically. That makes a kitchen scrap a workable ingredient for a lightweight metal, at least in a small lab test.

The work came from the lab of Bharat Gwalani, an assistant professor of materials science and engineering at North Carolina State University.

It was a first test on small rods, and the finished metal wasn’t measurably harder than plain magnesium. Its gain in strength showed up only in microscopic crush tests.

Magnesium is a light metal. A recent antenna design for Mars helicopters used a magnesium frame.

“Calcium is added to magnesium to improve its mechanical properties,” Gwalani said. “We wanted to see if we could use biogenic waste – eggshells – to produce the necessary calcium materials during the manufacturing process.”

Biogenic waste just means leftovers from living things. Eggshells already appear on lists of food leftovers that could be recovered and reused, and other labs have turned food waste into plastic.

Industry makes one of those compounds, calcium oxide, by heating limestone in industrial kilns until it gives off carbon dioxide.

Earlier teams had already blended eggshell powder into magnesium, either by melting the metal or by stirring the powder into its surface.

However, little was known about what happens to the shell inside the metal during a friction-based press like this one.

Gwalani’s co-authors included researchers at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, where first author Aniruddha Malakar now works, and at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi.

The eggshells came from ordinary households. The team washed them, dried them in an oven at about 300°F (150°C) for four hours, and ground them with a mortar and pestle.

Then they cut small grooves, each about an eighth of an inch (3 mm) wide, into a short magnesium cylinder about an inch (25.4 mm) across. The eggshell powder filled the grooves in the metal and made up roughly 8.4 percent of the block by volume.

That’s a pinch of shell in a lot of metal.

A die spinning 300 times a minute pressed into the block at about 3 inches (75 mm) a minute and squeezed it out as a rod. Friction and squeezing heated the metal to roughly 930°F (500°C), hot enough to soften it without melting it.

Most of the shell particles measured 2 to 4 micrometers across, far thinner than a human hair. They were spread evenly through the rod.

Metal is made of tiny crystals called grains. In a plain magnesium rod made the same way, the grains averaged 16 micrometers across. With eggshell mixed in, they averaged 8.

Smaller grains usually make a metal stronger. Even so, the eggshell rod wasn’t measurably harder than the plain one when the team pressed a diamond tip into its surface.

The eggshell’s effect appeared only after the metal started to give way. The researchers carved microscopic pillars out of grains pointing in the same direction in both metals. Then they crushed them.

Both kinds of pillar began to give way at about the same stress. Once they did, the eggshell pillars kept resisting harder as they squashed.

Their peak strength reached about 32,600 pounds per square inch (225 megapascals), compared with about 29,000 pounds per square inch (200 megapascals) for plain magnesium.

The team thinks the shell bits help tiny flaws in the metal’s crystals pile up as it deforms. The more of those flaws that build up, the harder the metal is to squash further.

The second finding was chemical. Calcium carbonate usually breaks apart into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide at about 1,650 to 1,740°F (900 to 950°C) under normal air pressure.

Inside the press, the metal reached only about 930°F (500°C). Several of the smallest shell fragments broke down, at least partly. The team established this by measuring calcium, oxygen and carbon across individual particles.

The researchers think the spots where shell met metal got much hotter than the overall reading. They suspect sudden swings in pressure helped too.

Near the edges of some particles, the measurements pointed to magnesium oxide. The likeliest source, the team concluded, was carbon dioxide from the broken-down shell reacting with the surrounding magnesium.

The reaction was patchy, though. Larger particles, a few micrometers or more across, stayed mostly unchanged. The finished rod held a mix of untouched shell, partly broken-down shell and areas rich in calcium oxide.

One compound didn’t form. That compound, Mg2Ca, is a compound of magnesium and calcium that can strengthen magnesium alloys, and the team didn’t detect it. The calcium stayed mostly locked up as calcium oxide.

The authors wrote that their goal was to understand what happens inside the metal, not to make the strongest possible material.

They tested only one spin speed and one feed rate. The team also didn’t measure whether the process uses less energy than making calcium compounds from rock, although Gwalani said it should.

“There are fewer steps,” Gwalani said. “You have a reliable, sustainable supply chain. Eggshells are inexpensive.”

Gwalani’s group in NC State’s Department of Materials Science and Engineering has also used the same kind of press to work magnetic powder into scrap aluminum.

The next step is to push the chemistry further. The authors suggested heating the shell powder before it goes in, running the press longer or hotter, or working in a sealed chamber with less oxygen.

Any of those might free the calcium from its oxide and get it into the magnesium itself, the step that this first test didn’t reach.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Magnesium and Alloys.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6397. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

#6395. The Sky Today on Sunday, November 8: Io and Callisto race across Jupiter

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Rising with the stars of western Leo shortly before midnight, bright Jupiter and its Galilean moons put on a show early this morning, better visible the farther east you’re located.

Jupiter is just under 5° northwest (to the upper right) of Regulus as they rise in the east. Fainter Mars stands roughly 3° above Jupiter. You’ll want your telescope trained on the gas giant soon after rising to catch the show, which begins at 1:29 A.M. EST as a shadow appears on the planet’s eastern limb. This is Io’s shadow — but don’t be fooled by the positions of the moons you see in your scope. The moon closest to Jupiter on the east is Callisto, while the moon just east of that is Io, whose shadow we see. Ganymede lies farthest east, while Europa is currently hidden behind the planet in an occultation. The latter appears from behind the eastern limb about 1:54 A.M. EST, not long before Callisto reaches the planet and begins a transit at 2:07 A.M. EST.

Keep an eye on Io and Europa: Io passes north of Europa at 2:23 A.M. EST, then heads into its own transit about 2:42 A.M. EST. Now the race is on, as Io approaches and then catches up with Callisto as the two moons transit, passing Callisto and moving west of it within half an hour. The two moons and Io’s shadow continue to transit until 3:45 A.M. EST, when Io’s shadow leaves the western limb, and Io takes about an hour and a quarter longer before egress. Callisto continues trundling along, finally finishing its transit about 5:51 A.M. CST, with the sky now starting to brighten with twilight in the Midwest.

#6394. Can weight-loss drugs protect the brain? The evidence is complicated

A new review examines whether GLP-1 weight-loss drugs could preserve memory and why their potential benefits for brain health remain uncertain.

Semaglutide can help people lose weight and lower cardiovascular risk. But can it also help preserve memory and thinking skills?

That question sits at the center of a new review covering nearly 200 preclinical studies and some of the largest clinical trials ever run on these medications.

The short version: maybe. The honest version: we still don’t know how, or even if.

The review was led by Stina Börchers and Christoffer Clemmensen at the University of Copenhagen. What they’ve assembled is part map, part warning label.

Look at population-level studies and the picture is seductive.

Trawl through insurance databases and clinical registries and you’ll find that people with type 2 diabetes taking GLP-1 receptor agonists consistently develop dementia at lower rates than those on other glucose-lowering therapies.

The REWIND trial flagged a 14% lower hazard of substantial cognitive decline with dulaglutide. Headlines practically write themselves.

Cognition was an exploratory outcome in REWIND. The 14% reduction emerged after a post hoc adjustment for participants’ baseline cognitive scores.

A meta-analysis pooling five randomized clinical trials, 7,732 adults with type 2 diabetes in total, found no clear improvement in global cognitive performance.

The observational findings remain promising, but randomized trials have not established a clear cognitive benefit.

The sharpest disappointments came from Alzheimer’s research. ELAD tested liraglutide in 204 people with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer’s for a year.

It missed its primary endpoint, which measured brain glucose metabolism.

Some MRI measures and a secondary cognitive outcome favored liraglutide, but measures of daily functioning and overall clinical severity did not show significant benefits.

EVOKE and EVOKE+ went much bigger. These phase 3 trials enrolled 3,808 participants with mild cognitive impairment or early Alzheimer’s.

Participants were assigned to oral semaglutide, with a target dose of 14 mg daily, or placebo for two years.

The drug didn’t slow decline on the Clinical Dementia Rating scale and it didn’t help with daily functioning.

It did nudge some biomarkers, though – roughly 10% reductions in cerebrospinal fluid levels of phosphorylated tau and neurogranin.

But biomarker movement, by itself, is not evidence that a disease is being modified.

GLP-1 receptors are sprinkled across brain regions you’d want a cognition drug to reach – hippocampus, amygdala, prefrontal cortex, substantia nigra.

Preclinical work shows effects on synaptic plasticity and neurotrophic signaling through CREB and BDNF pathways. On paper, the biology is there.

In practice, these drugs are large peptide molecules. They don’t cross the blood-brain barrier easily.

Most evidence suggests they reach circumventricular organs – spots where capillaries are naturally leaky – and parts of the brainstem.

Whether these drugs ever touch the hippocampus in pharmacologically relevant concentrations depends on the compound, the species, the dose, and the detection method. Nobody has a clean answer.

This raises a question about GLP-1 drugs and the brain: Could any cognitive benefits come indirectly from better metabolic health?

They could be side effects of side effects – downstream consequences of tighter blood sugar, less inflammation, healthier blood vessels, better sleep.

Semaglutide cut cardiovascular events by 20% in the SELECT trial. It reduced major kidney outcomes by 24% in FLOW.

Tirzepatide dramatically improved obstructive sleep apnea in the SURMOUNT-OSA trials. Every one of those improvements could benefit the brain indirectly.

“We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit,” Börchers said.

Obesity and diabetes can affect attention, planning, and processing speed.

Alzheimer’s disease often affects the ability to remember events and experiences early in its course. These patterns can overlap, but their underlying causes and responses to treatment may differ.

These are not the same problem dressed in different clothes. They arise from different biology.

A drug that might improve executive function in someone with metabolic syndrome is not necessarily going to rescue memory in someone with amyloid plaques.

Worse, the relationship between blood sugar and cognition runs in both directions.

Hypoglycemia damages thinking. But cognitive impairment also makes dangerous blood sugar crashes more likely. Picking apart cause and effect inside that loop is a nightmare.

Rapid weight loss can reduce muscle mass, potentially worsening frailty in vulnerable older adults.

It can cause dehydration, malnutrition, and reduced protein intake. Fatigue shows up more often with incretin-based therapies than with placebo.

In people already teetering toward frailty, these side effects could erase whatever cognitive benefit the metabolic improvements might deliver.

The review calls for trials that track body composition, nutritional status, and treatment tolerability alongside cognition.

Newer treatments combine GLP-1 activity with effects on GIP, glucagon, or amylin pathways. Different combinations may have different effects on brain function.

GIPR agonism and antagonism, for instance, appear to activate entirely different brain mechanisms rather than simply opposing each other.

Brain-penetrant peptides and small-molecule agonists could eventually bypass the blood-brain barrier problem altogether.

The OxSENSE study is already testing semaglutide’s acute effects on reward sensitivity, memory, and emotional processing in healthy adults.

“Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function,” Clemmensen said.

“By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function.”

The review is published in the journal Science.

#6393. Scientists designed a new way to hunt for signs of life in space using electricity and artificial intelligence

An electrical sensor told mirror-image amino acids apart, one molecule at a time, taking a step toward small instruments that can look for signs of life.

Your left and right hands are made of the same parts, yet a left hand won’t fit properly into a right glove. Many of the molecules in living things come in the same two mirror-image versions, and life on Earth builds its proteins overwhelmingly from just one of them.

A team led by researchers in Japan has now told those two versions apart, one molecule at a time, using only an electrical current.

The sensor could one day help a small spacecraft instrument look for that lopsided mix on another world. The team also tested it on extracts from a meteorite and from desert soil, where it caught the broad pattern but missed on several details.

Takahito Ohshiro and Masateru Taniguchi of the University of Osaka led the work with colleagues at Georgia Tech, NASA Goddard, MIT and the University of Chicago. Everything so far has happened in a lab, and no flight instrument exists yet.

Amino acids, the small molecules that link up into proteins, mostly come in mirror images, a left-handed form and a right-handed form. Scientists label them L and D. Chemistry without life tends to make the two in equal amounts, while living things lean heavily toward one, the L form.

A strong tilt toward one hand is therefore a possible sign of biology. Some researchers have proposed an excess of more than 20 percent in several amino acids as a threshold that would point to life.

Meteorites once seemed to carry such a tilt, but those results are now generally blamed on contamination from Earth. Samples brought back from the asteroids Ryugu and Bennu showed roughly equal mixes.

In an interview with Earth.com, Taniguchi was careful about what the measurement can show. “Importantly, chirality should not be viewed as proof of life by itself,” Taniguchi said.

“It would become much more powerful when combined with molecular identity, abundance, chemical context, and other biosignatures.”

The sensor starts as a thin gold wire that is pulled until it snaps. The two broken tips sit a little more than half a billionth of a meter apart. That’s more than 100,000 times narrower than a human hair.

A small voltage pushes a trickle of current across that gap. When an amino acid drifts in, the current jumps for a few thousandths of a second, then drops back.

Each jump has a shape, and the L and D forms of the same amino acid leave slightly different shapes. A machine-learning program trained on thousands of these spikes learned to sort them.

“We are not measuring only an average signal from a large population of molecules,” Taniguchi said.

Standard lab methods for telling the two mirror-image molecules apart rely on light or chemical reagents. The electrical approach needs neither. Taniguchi said spacecraft instruments have to be small, sturdy, sensitive and energy-efficient, and dropping the optics could help with that.

The team tested 19 amino acids that come in both forms. Working from a single spike, the program picked the right form about 88 percent of the time on average. The hardest pair, glutamine, came in at 78 percent, and the easiest, isoleucine, at 97 percent.

One spike is a weak basis for a verdict, and a five-minute run collects hundreds. By the team’s calculation, a program that is right 90 percent of the time on each spike would be right 99.9 percent of the time after 16 spikes.

A harder test asked the program to name both the amino acid and its hand from all 39 possible forms at once. It was right about half the time, far better than the 1-in-39 rate that a guess would give.

Mixtures were harder still. In test solutions holding four or five amino acids, some counted shares landed close to the true values. One was off by 56 percent.

Next came real samples. The team ran extracts from a fragment of the Murchison meteorite, supplied by the Smithsonian. It also tested soil from two sites in Chile’s Atacama Desert, a Mars-like environment. A standard lab instrument analyzed the same extracts for comparison.

The program only counted spikes it was confident about, and it rejected about 93 percent of the spikes from a blank sample that contained no extract.

Both methods found glycine to be the most common amino acid in the meteorite, at 48 percent by the sensor and 63 percent by the standard instrument.

Other results drifted. The sensor put serine at nearly 12 percent of the meteorite’s amino acids, compared with well under 1 percent by the standard method. It also found no glutamic acid at all in either desert soil.

For handedness, the sensor matched the standard method on aspartic acid in the meteorite, but not on alanine or valine.

“In that sense, the real samples were not only a demonstration of the technology, but also an important test of its current limits,” Taniguchi told Earth.com.

The authors wrote that the method should be treated as a targeted tool for a shortlist of known molecules, not a full chemical inventory. It can’t yet recognize a molecule it wasn’t trained on, and a messy natural sample adds background signals that blur the counts.

Taniguchi listed what a flight version would need. It would have to measure amounts more accurately, flag unfamiliar molecules, prepare its own samples and keep out contamination from Earth.

It would also need shrunken electronics that survive vibration, radiation and temperature swings.

“Ultimately, we envision a compact instrument in which sample preparation, single-molecule electrical detection, and AI-based molecular identification operate as one system,” Taniguchi said.

Only a working prototype can show whether the sensor works away from a clean lab bench, on a sample from Mars, an icy moon or an asteroid.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6392. Nov. 8, 1656: The birth of Edmond Halley

It’s been said that the general public knows three astronomical objects: the Moon, the rings of Saturn, and Halley’s Comet. English astronomer Edmond Halley, born Nov. 8, 1656, didn’t discover the object named for him. In fact, he never even saw it — but his mathematical prediction of its return in 1758 guaranteed his place in history.

Halley was a friend of Isaac Newton and used Newton’s theory of gravity and to calculate “his” comet’s orbit. In fact, Halley published at his own expense the book Newton wrote explaining the theory, Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica. In 1676, Halley sailed to the island of St. Helena in the South Atlantic Ocean and spent a year measuring stellar positions, the result of which was the first catalog of the southern sky.

Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused.

Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science.

I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma.

That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. I went to the party, but I texted my mom saying I should come home because I really wasn't feeling well, which was not usual for me at all. That night I asked my mom to sleep with me because I just felt terrible.

That was Saturday. By Sunday night, the only position that I could get comfortable in was my mom holding me like a baby. My mom just held me all weekend. My whole body just hurt and I started feeling like I couldn't breathe properly. That got way worse Monday morning.

We were waiting for my pediatrician to open up and my mom suggested taking a shower, saying, "Maybe that will help you feel a bit better before we go to the doctor." She had to help me take a shower because I was so weak, I couldn't stand by myself. She stepped away for a second just to grab a towel and said that when she came back, my lips were turning gray and my eyes were starting to look sunken in. She knew that something was not right so she called my dad, who was at the grocery store, and told him to just leave everything, that we need to get to the hospital.

Allen was put on life support and had to be intubated for five weeks after getting sick with flu.

Our local hospital is just a small rural hospital — everybody gets transferred out. They diagnosed me with double pneumonia and then sent me to a different hospital 30 minutes away that specialized more in kids.

My dad rode with me in the ambulance while my mom went home and grabbed a few things — she thought we'd just be there for a few days. By the time we got to the second hospital, I was in respiratory distress. They wanted to intubate me straight away but were waiting until my mom got there so she could talk to me — my dad did the best he could, but my dad didn't know how to calm me down.

I don't think the doctors even told me that they were putting me to sleep. My mom had to be the one to tell me. I remember being very scared. They put this mask on my face for the BiPAP [bilevel positive airway pressure machine, which delivers pressurized air to a patient] and I felt like that was suffocating me. It didn't feel like it was helping at all, which, I guess, at that point, it wasn't. They were just trying everything they could. I was begging them to take it off of me, crying and just saying, "one minute, just take it off for one minute."

Finally my mom tried to calm me down and she's like, "They're gonna have to put you to sleep now." I remember her telling me, "You're just gonna go to sleep for like a couple of hours and then you're gonna wake up and you're gonna feel a lot better."

My mom had to leave the room while they were doing that. As she was walking out the door, the last thing I said was "Mom" and then I put my hands in a heart shape. That was the last thing I did and the last time my mom heard my voice for five weeks.

After I was intubated, things got worse. I had to be put on life support so needed to be moved to a bigger hospital in St. Louis, Missouri. The flight team came to evaluate me and they later told me they didn't think they were ever going to get me to Saint Louis. They thought I wasn't going to make the trip. But they said my mom was begging them to help me, everyone in my family was begging them, so they did everything they could to get me on the helicopter. They worked on me for several hours — every time they tried to move me something would go wrong — but eventually they got me there.

The doctors had to call my parents to get permission to do surgery and put me on life support. My mom said that every time she heard my dad's phone ring, she thought they were calling to tell them that I didn't make it. They were told twice that it was more than likely I was going to pass than make it. They were trying to prepare my parents that I wasn't going to make it.

After getting out of hospital, it took years for Allen to recover, eventually having part of her lung removed that had been badly damaged by the virus.

I woke up five weeks later, and it was very confusing. Everybody was told if I asked what day it was, just to tell me the day of the week. When someone accidentally told me the date, I started crying because my aunt was supposed to be getting married a few weeks later and I was worried about being at her wedding. My mom wasn't there, so my dad had to calm me down and then he told me the wedding had been pushed to October so I could be there.

The second thing I was worried about was that I was supposed to take a test on the Constitution and that I'd missed it. I ended up taking it in the hospital. I was there for 93 days. I got out the very last week of school, so I got to go in on the last day of school and surprise my classmates and my teachers.

That summer, I didn't really do anything besides go to doctor's appointments. I was doing physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy — literally all my time was spent at the hospital in therapy. I'd missed three months of school, but I got to start eighth grade with all my friends, and I ended up playing basketball again. But the next several years was a lot of hard work of trying to get back to my normal.

It probably took the rest of junior high and high school to get back to how I would have been before. It was a very long process and during that time I got sick a lot, so I ended up back in the hospital several times. And it was hard going through that as a teenager — I felt like everybody else is living their normal life, and I felt like I missed out on a lot. Looking back now, I still feel like I did miss out a lot. But I think we made the best of the circumstances.

During COVID, when I was 22, I kept getting sick, and the doctors finally told me that part of my lung was so damaged from the flu it was causing infections, so they gave me an option of getting part of my lung removed. It was a major surgery, but I did it and that was probably the best decision I ever made, because it's been five years and I have not been in the hospital once.

I moved to Florida about three years ago, and I started working as a medical assistant in a pulmonary clinic. This semester I got accepted into respiratory therapy school, so for the next two years, I'm going to be in school for respiratory therapy. It's kind of a full circle moment, to come back into the medical field, because there was a point in my life where everybody was asking me, "Oh, do you want to be a doctor? Do you want to be a nurse?" And I'm like, "Absolutely not." I was still so sick that I was there all the time. I never wanted to be there.

I went to college and I got a degree in criminal justice, but I never really knew what I wanted to do. I ended up getting a job at our local hospital — that first hospital that I went to. Every time they put me in the ER I just loved being there. That job made me realize that this is what I wanted to do.

When people hear my story, they don't realize that if I don't tell the end — after the hospital until now — they don't realize that my life didn't go back to normal after. It's taken 10 years. And it's hard. Some of the other family members that we've gotten to know through Families Fighting Flu, it's difficult listening to their stories. Sometimes I feel like I have this survivor's guilt. Their stories sound exactly like mine — but their kids didn't make it.

Before I got sick I got the flu shot every year, but that year we just got busy and it got put on the back burner. Since getting sick I have always made it a priority to get the flu shot every year. I know it is not a guarantee that I will never get the flu again — but hopefully it will reduce the chances of it ever getting that bad again.

With thanks to Families Fighting Flu, a non-profit organization that promotes flu vaccination and raises awareness of the severity of the infectious disease through families that have been affected.

#6389. Plant-based dairy swaps may leave a key nutrient behind

A UK modeling study suggests replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives could deepen iodine shortfalls, especially among teenage girls and women.

Plant-based milk, yogurt and cheese make it easy to cut back on dairy without rethinking every meal.

In the UK, though, dairy is one of the main places people get iodine, a mineral the body uses to make thyroid hormones. Most plant-based versions contain very little of it.

A new modeling study estimates that swapping about a third of dairy for store-bought plant-based products would leave more teenage girls and young women short of iodine.

The same model also tested a fix, and adding iodine to both the plant-based products and bread kept every age group at least as well supplied as before.

Researchers at the University of Surrey and Queen’s University Belfast asked no one to change their diet.

The study, led by Katie Nicol, used real food diaries and calculated how much of four vitamins and minerals people would get if some of their dairy were replaced.

“With the rise in plant-based alternative foods, we need to know whether they are like-for-like replacements for the micronutrients that are found in dairy products,” said Nicol.

Cow’s milk in the UK is rich in iodine partly because farmers add it to cattle feed to keep animals healthy. Iodine-containing disinfectants used in dairy production add to it.

Many countries add iodine to table salt. The UK doesn’t have that policy, and iodized salt is hard to find in British shops, so dairy has become the country’s main iodine source.

In the team’s earlier survey of UK supermarkets, only 12% of plant-based alternatives had added iodine, and even those often contained less than cow’s milk.

Sarah Bath, an associate professor in public health nutrition at the University of Surrey, was also involved in the study.

“People may also be unaware of the importance of iodine, which is needed to make thyroid hormones to regulate our metabolism, support healthy growth and brain development,” said Bath.

The team started with the UK’s National Diet and Nutrition Survey.

Between 2016 and 2019, the survey asked 3,558 people, from 18-month-olds to adults up to 100, to write down everything they ate for four days.

The researchers focused on the 3,095 people who ate some dairy during those days, since there’s nothing to swap in a diet without it.

On an average day, these people had about 237 grams of milk, cheese and yogurt.

The team then replaced that dairy, gram for gram, with plant-based versions from UK supermarket websites. Each one was picked at random, so the results reflected how widely those products vary.

The researchers tested four levels of change, replacing 20%, 35%, 50% or all of a person’s dairy. The first two match the UK climate plan’s call to cut meat and dairy by 20% by 2030 and 35% by 2050.

The 50% level reflects international advice to cut animal foods worldwide by more than half. Dairy contributes substantially to greenhouse gas emissions.

Teenage girls were the worst off from the start, and those aged 14 to 18 ate less dairy than any other group.

The team estimated that 54% of them fell short of the daily iodine benchmark nutritionists use to judge whether a group is getting enough.

In a population with enough iodine, only about 2% to 3% of people would fall below that line.

The model estimates that replacing just over a third of their dairy would push the share of teenage girls falling short to 65%.

For women of childbearing age, 19 to 49, it would climb from 32% to 42%.

The authors wrote that iodine is especially important during pregnancy, infancy and adolescence.

If all dairy were replaced, the model estimates that 80% of teenage girls and 72% of teenage boys would fall short.

Young children, teenagers and adult women had the biggest drops overall.

Calcium, riboflavin (a B vitamin) and vitamin B12 intakes also fell, but shortfalls became more common only when half or all of the dairy was replaced. Iodine was the most sensitive of the four.

Next, the team tested three fixes. The first required every plant-based product to contain all four nutrients, at the minimum level needed to be labeled a source of each one.

The requirement kept average intakes steady, but it didn’t fix the shortfall teenage girls already had. Between 56% and 59% of them still fell below the iodine benchmark.

The second option was bread, which six in 10 people in the survey ate. Australia and New Zealand already require bakers to use iodized salt in bread.

In the model, doing the same with all commercially made bread cut the share of teenage girls short on iodine from 54% to 37%.

For women aged 19 to 49, iodized bread helped less as dairy disappeared.

Their shortfall dropped from 32% to 24% when a fifth of their dairy was replaced, but rose to 44% once all of it was gone.

The best results came from doing both. With iodine added to plant-based products and to bread, every age group kept or improved its iodine supply, even with no dairy at all.

None of the policies raised the share of any group getting too much iodine.

“Nutrition policy must evolve in tandem with environmental targets; however, it is important that shifts towards more sustainable diets do not compromise on public health,” Nicol said.

The study is a set of calculations, not a trial in which people changed what they ate. It assumes everyone shifts in the same way, even though interest in plant-based products varies with age, sex and culture.

Without sales figures, the model gave every product the same chance of being picked, though real shoppers don’t buy them equally.

The product data also come from a 2020 survey, and recipes in this market may change.

Nor did the team look at how well the body absorbs nutrients from fortified foods. People who ate no dairy at all, 13% of the survey, were left out, so it’s unknown how fortification would affect them.

Whether real diets will shift the way the model assumes remains an open question.

The authors called for continued tracking of what people eat, and how much of each nutrient they get, as the food supply keeps changing.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet Planetary Health.

#6388. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

#6386. Gemini North reveals Twin Spirits in Pegasus

Three high school students in the Project Hōkūlani internship at Gemini North on Maunakea, Hawaii, chose this pair of clashing spirals, cataloged collectively as NGC 7253 or Arp 278, for imaging with the 8.1-meter telescope. It captured this photo — the most detailed ever taken of these galaxies — in October 2025. The students selected this target because it’s in a traditional Hawaiian constellation, Ka Lupe o Kawelo, or the Kite of Kawelo, located in Pegasus. In June 2026, three more interns gave the pair of galaxies a new name: Nā ʻUhane Māhoe Huki Pū i ke Ola, meaning “the Twin Spirits Pulling Together Creating Life” in Hawaiian. The title refers to the way that, over billions of years, the two galaxies will merge, sparking the formation of new stars and planets.

#6385. The Sky Today on Monday, November 9: Chase Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 8: Io and Callisto race across Jupiter

Dark skies make tonight the perfect opportunity to try spotting Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS, still nearly 50° above the western horizon two hours after sunset.

Glowing around 10th magnitude, the comet is currently located in far northern Aquila, near the Eagle’s border with Sagitta the Arrow. You can use Aquila’s bright luminary, Altair, to guide your way — the comet floats 7.7° north-northeast of this star. A closer but fainter guide is 4th-magnitude Alpha (α) Sagittae, just 2.3° north of the comet’s position tonight. Even a small scope will nab you the comet, but larger apertures will yield better views. Under high magnification, look at the comet’s southern side, which should be sharper as it plows into the solar wind.

Not far from Hartley-IRAS’ position is the famous Coathanger asterism, located in Vulpecula the Fox. Cataloged as Collinder 399, you’ll find it roughly 5° northwest of the comet’s position, or about 4° northwest of Alpha Sge. Visible in binoculars or any telescope (in this case, lower magnification is better), you’ll immediately see why this star pattern bears its name. It looks exactly like its namesake, with a line of stars bisected by a small curve extending to the south. At the Coathanger’s eastern edge lies the open cluster NGC 6802.

A new study points to testosterone and proteins in the skin as reasons why males and females experience temperatures differently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's a common observation that women often prefer warmer temperatures and feel cold more easily than men do, and the same trend appears among females of other species. Now, a study offers new clues as to what drives this preference — and testosterone may play a part.

Skin carries sensors to detect heat and cold that influence each organism's decision to stay in or move out of an environment. The new study, published Oct. 28 in the Journal of Physiology, found that these sensors activate at higher temperatures in female mice, which appears to shift their preferred temperature roughly 7 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) higher than that of male mice. Testosterone seems to influence this difference in activation.

"You could say it's just a cute observation of no particular importance," said study co-author Peter McNaughton, a pharmacologist at King's College London who studies pain, thermal sensation and thermoregulation. "[But] it's got practical ramifications," in that it might be important in designing buildings and spaces that accommodate people, he told Live Science.

Proteins in the skin's nerve endings activate in response to warmth or cold. "You can look at them like little electrical generators in the nerve endings," said Dr. Michael Caterina, a neuroscientist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the research.

When activated, these proteins allow charged ions to enter sensory nerve cells, which, in turn, transmit electrical signals to the brain. The circuits a given nerve cell connects to determines our perception of heat or cold, Caterina told Live Science.

Beyond humans, it is known that many female animals, including mice and birds, prefer slightly warmer temperatures than their male counterparts do. So the researchers set up an experiment to investigate these differences.

They put 30 male and 27 female mice on two adjacent plates of different temperatures — one at 91.4 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius) and another that varied between lower and higher temperatures. A camera tracked the mice's movements and calculated how much time they spent on each plate.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both male and female mice spent more time at the 91.4 F plate when the second plate was cooler. However, when put next to a plate measuring 100.4 F (38 C), female mice spent significantly more time on the warmer plate than male mice did. The average preferred surface temperature was approximately 89.6 F (32 C) for male mice and 96.8 F (36 C) for female mice.

"Since the top of the cage was completely open, there was no question of the air temperature affecting the mice," McNaughton said, so the preference was driven solely by the sensors in their skin. The researchers also measured the internal and skin temperatures of the mice and confirmed that there were no significant differences between the sexes on those fronts.

The scientists explored what would happen if they genetically deleted the warmth-detector protein. In male mice, this reduced their avoidance of the warmer plate, suggesting this protein normally sends a signal that discourages them from staying on warmer surfaces. The mice's preferred temperature also rose to about 95 F (35 C), closer to that of females.

The study suggests that testosterone somehow tweaks the function of heat-sensing nerves in the skin.

In female mice, deleting or blocking the protein did not have any significant effect.

The team then tried eliminating or blocking the coolness-detecting protein, finding that males and females didn't avoid the cool plates as strongly as they did before. Female mice also spent less time on the warmer plates, but males' preference for the warmer plates didn't change.

"Females are a little bit more responsive to activation of the cold receptor," Caterina said, "and a little bit less responsive to activation of the warmer receptor." That's despite the temperature-sensing neurons in both sets of mice working identically, the team found.

The researchers suspected that sex hormones might help to explain this difference.

They gave a group of male mice a drug that blocks the production of testosterone. Weeks after the treatment, these mice spent more time on the 38 C plate than males with normal testosterone. Meanwhile, female mice given testosterone lost their preference for warmer temperatures.

Interestingly, giving male mice female hormones, including forms of estrogen and progesterone, did not affect their temperature preferences. And blocking the hormones in female mice also had no effect. These hormones are known to influence other aspects of temperature regulation in the body, though, such as heat dissipation through the skin; but in this case, they didn't seem to affect animals' perception of temperature.

"So it really seems as though testosterone is the most important determinant," McNaughton said. But these changes were only partial; testosterone did not completely reverse the differences between the sexes. "So there is something else going on that we weren't able to identify," he added.

The exact mechanism for how testosterone impacts the sensor proteins is not clear. Because the effect happened over weeks, researchers suggested that it did not directly affect the temperature-sensing proteins. It might instead act indirectly by influencing the activity of genes, but further studies would be needed to confirm this idea.

Although the researchers did not conduct any tests in humans, McNaughton noted that the same sensor proteins are present in people and that studies with humans suggest that they behave in a similar way.

This research provides "valuable information" for understanding how the proteins responsible for sensing temperature work, Caterina said. Understanding these mechanisms could be useful for studying conditions like neuropathic pain, in which people's sensitivity to heat and cold is enhanced.

"What kinds of signals create our daily experiences around temperature is by itself very important," he told Live Science. "It's a big part of understanding ourselves as living beings."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Vilar, B., & McNaughton, P. A. (2026). TRPM8 and TRPM2 ion channels determine sex differences in thermal preference in mice. The Journal of Physiology. https://doi.org/10.1113/jp288076

Zunnash Khan is a mechatronics engineer and a science journalist from Pakistan. She has written for Science, The Scientist and Brainfacts.org, among other outlets.

#6382. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

Monday, November 9New Moon occurs at 2:02 A.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:38 A.M.Sunset: 4:49 P.M.Moonrise: 7:12 A.M.Moonset: 4:40 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (1%)

Tuesday, November 10The waxing crescent Moon passes 0.3° south of Antares at midnight EST, although the pair is not visible at that time. You can catch our satellite setting in the west around sunset, although it will likely disappear before Antares pops out of the twilight only shortly before the star itself sets as well.

Sunrise: 6:39 A.M.Sunset: 4:48 P.M.Moonrise: 8:15 A.M.Moonset: 5:19 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (4%)
